title: ASP.NET Core and EF Core
blurb: DI lifetimes, the middleware pipeline, model binding, configuration, EF Core. The two most reliably asked .NET interview questions live in here.

questions.q: What is the difference between Singleton, Scoped and Transient?
choices: Singleton: one per request. Scoped: one per application. Transient: one per calling thread
Singleton: one for the app's lifetime. Scoped: one per request. Transient: new on each resolve
They set thread safety: Singleton is locked, Scoped is per thread, Transient is unsynchronised
They set GC behaviour: Singleton is never collected, Scoped and Transient are collected early
questions.why: Lifetimes decide how many instances the container creates, not how they are locked or collected. DbContext is scoped because it tracks changes for one unit of work. Stateless helpers can be singletons, which must then be thread-safe on their own. Transient suits cheap objects with no shared state.
questions.asked: The single most asked .NET interview question. Know it cold.

questions.q: What is a captive dependency?
choices: Two services that depend on each other, so the container can never finish building either
A service registered twice with different lifetimes, so the last registration silently wins
A longer-lived service holding a shorter-lived one, such as a singleton capturing a DbContext
A dependency created with `new` inside a service, so the container cannot manage its lifetime
questions.why: In Development, scope validation is on and the host throws at startup ("Cannot consume scoped service from singleton"). In Production validation is off by default, so the scoped object is silently captured on first resolution and shared by every request, which is neither thread-safe nor correct. Inject IServiceScopeFactory and create a scope per unit of work.
questions.asked: The natural depth follow-up to the lifetimes question, and it separates real experience from memorisation.

questions.q: Why does the order of `app.Use...` calls matter?
choices: It does not: ASP.NET Core sorts the built-in middleware into a safe order at startup
Middleware forms an ordered pipeline; each one can short-circuit or pass to the next
Only the first and last calls matter, because the middle ones run in parallel
Order matters only for authentication; every other middleware can go anywhere
questions.why: Each middleware wraps the ones registered after it. UseAuthentication must come before UseAuthorization, both before the endpoints, and UseCors before anything that would short-circuit a preflight. Nothing re-sorts them for you, and a wrong order usually fails silently rather than crashing.
questions.asked: The second most asked .NET question. Expect to be asked to place a few in order.

questions.q: How does a middleware short-circuit the pipeline?
choices: By throwing an OperationCanceledException, which stops the pipeline cleanly
By returning false from InvokeAsync, which tells the host to stop there
By writing a response and not calling `await next(context)`
By calling `context.Abort()`, which completes the request normally
questions.why: Not calling `next` means nothing later in the pipeline runs. That is how authorisation returns 401 without reaching your endpoint and how caching serves a hit. `Abort()` resets the connection rather than sending a response, and a thrown exception becomes an error. Calling next after writing the response is a common bug: the headers are already sent.
questions.asked: Tests whether you could write a middleware yourself, not only configure the built-in ones.

questions.q: With the default WebApplication builder, where is configuration read from, and in what order?
choices: Environment variables, then appsettings.{Environment}.json, then appsettings.json; first found wins
appsettings.json only, unless you call AddEnvironmentVariables yourself, and then variables win
appsettings.json, appsettings.{Environment}.json, user secrets (Development only), env vars, CLI
Command line, then environment variables, then the JSON files; a key set earlier cannot change
questions.why: Later providers override earlier ones, which is what lets a container override a file value with an environment variable, and the command line override both. User secrets are added only in Development. The default builder already adds environment variables. Nested keys use `Section__Key` in environment variables.
questions.asked: Explains "why is production using the wrong connection string", which is a real debugging question.

questions.q: What is the difference between `IOptions<T>`, `IOptionsSnapshot<T>` and `IOptionsMonitor<T>`?
choices: IOptions re-reads on each access; IOptionsSnapshot caches for the app's life; IOptionsMonitor is for logs
IOptions is a singleton read once; IOptionsSnapshot is re-read per request; IOptionsMonitor notifies changes
IOptions is for secrets; IOptionsSnapshot is for appsettings.json; IOptionsMonitor is for environment variables
All three behave the same at runtime; they differ only in the package and namespace they come from
questions.why: If a config change should take effect without a restart, IOptions will not see it. IOptionsSnapshot is scoped, so it cannot be injected into a singleton (a captive dependency); IOptionsMonitor is a singleton with `CurrentValue` and `OnChange`, which is the one to use there. None of them is tied to a configuration source.
questions.asked: A standard mid-level .NET question; the singleton follow-up shows whether you have used it.

questions.q: In a controller marked `[ApiController]`, what happens when the request body fails validation?
choices: Nothing automatic: the action must check ModelState.IsValid itself before using the input
The model binder throws, and the developer exception page shows the validation errors
An automatic 400 with a ValidationProblemDetails body is returned before the action runs
The invalid fields are reset to defaults and the action runs as if the input were valid
questions.why: `[ApiController]` adds a filter that short-circuits invalid model state with a 400 and a ValidationProblemDetails body. Without the attribute, or in a minimal API without the opt-in validation added in .NET 10, you check yourself, which is what the first choice describes. Knowing which applies is what the question is testing.
questions.asked: Checks whether you know what the framework does for you and where it stops.

questions.q: What is model binding?
choices: Binding a Razor view to a model so that edits in the view update the model object
Mapping an entity class to a database table, including its columns and relations
Serialising the action's return value into JSON in the format the client asked for
Mapping route values, query string, headers and body onto action parameters
questions.why: The bug it causes: a complex type binds from the body by default, a simple type from the route or query. Getting a null parameter usually means the value was not where the binder looked, hence `[FromBody]`, `[FromQuery]` and friends. Table mapping is EF Core, and writing the response is output formatting.
questions.asked: Definitional, but the null-parameter bug is the practical follow-up.

questions.q: What is ProblemDetails?
choices: A structured logging format that records the exception type, message and stack trace
The standard error body from RFC 9457 (formerly 7807): type, title, status, detail
The base exception class that ASP.NET Core maps to HTTP status codes for you
The JSON body a health check endpoint returns when a dependency is unhealthy
questions.why: Using the standard shape means clients and tooling can parse errors without bespoke code. `AddProblemDetails()` plus the exception handler middleware produce it for unhandled errors, rather than a try/catch in every action. It is a response format, not an exception type or a log format.
questions.asked: Shows you design consistent error responses instead of ad-hoc strings.

questions.q: What does EF Core's change tracker do?
choices: Logs every query the context runs, so that data access can be audited later
Caches query results between requests, so repeated reads skip the database
Records which migrations have been applied, so the schema always matches the model
Records original values of loaded entities, so SaveChanges can write UPDATEs
questions.why: It is why you can change a loaded entity and call SaveChanges with no explicit update: EF compares current values with the snapshot. It does not cache across requests (each context is short-lived), and migrations history lives in a table. For read-only queries `AsNoTracking()` skips the bookkeeping.
questions.asked: The follow-up is always AsNoTracking, an easy, concrete performance win to mention.

questions.q: What typically causes an N+1 query pattern in EF Core?
choices: Reading a navigation property with default settings, which loads it once per row
Calling SaveChanges in a loop, which re-runs the original query for each entity
Lazy-loading proxies being enabled, or a query issued inside a loop over results
Registering the DbContext as transient, so each entity gets its own query
questions.why: Lazy loading is off by default in EF Core: with default settings an unloaded navigation is just null (a NullReferenceException, not N+1). The extra queries appear when proxies are switched on, or when your code queries inside a loop. Fix it with `Include`, a `Select` projection or a split query, and log the generated SQL in development to see it.
questions.asked: Tests whether you know EF Core defaults, not only the N+1 definition.

questions.q: Why is DbContext registered as Scoped?
choices: It is expensive to construct, so one per request is the cheapest safe option
It is not thread-safe and represents one unit of work, so one per request fits
It keeps its database connection open for the whole request to avoid reconnecting
EF Core migrations require it and fail at design time for other lifetimes
questions.why: Two concurrent requests sharing a context would corrupt the change tracker. Construction is cheap (and `AddDbContextPool` reuses instances when it matters), and connections are opened per operation and pooled by ADO.NET. For background work you create your own scope or context rather than borrowing the request's.
questions.asked: Connects DI lifetimes to a concrete type; the background-work follow-up is common.

questions.q: What is a migration in EF Core?
choices: A generated C# class describing a schema change, checked in and applied in order
A data import script that copies rows from one environment's database to another
A change to the model classes that EF applies to the database on the next start
A snapshot backup of the database taken before a deploy, used for rolling back
questions.why: `dotnet ef migrations add` scaffolds it from model changes and `database update` applies it. Model changes alone do nothing to the database until a migration is generated and applied. In production, migrating at startup is convenient and risky: a failed migration takes the app down and multiple instances race.
questions.asked: Basic EF workflow; the production-apply follow-up is where experience shows.

questions.q: What is the difference between a minimal API and a controller-based API?
choices: Minimal APIs cannot use dependency injection, so they suit only stateless endpoints
Controllers are deprecated since .NET 8 and remain only for backwards compatibility
Minimal APIs cannot return JSON directly and need a controller to serialise it
Minimal APIs map handlers directly; controllers add conventions and filters
questions.why: Both are first-class and share routing, DI, auth and model binding. Minimal APIs suit small services and read quickly; controllers earn their keep on large surfaces with cross-cutting filters and conventions. Minimal API handlers take services as parameters and return JSON by default.
questions.asked: Checks you are current; "controllers are legacy" and "minimal APIs are toys" are both wrong.

questions.q: How should long-running work triggered by a request be handled?
choices: Await it in the action, and raise the server's request timeout far enough to cover it
Start it with async void so the request returns while the work continues
Run it on a new Thread so it outlives the request and its pipeline
Queue it, return 202 Accepted with a status URL, and process it in the background
questions.why: Holding a request open ties up resources, hits proxy timeouts and dies with the deploy. A hosted service reading from a durable queue survives restarts. Async void and raw threads are fire-and-forget: their failures go unobserved and the work is lost when the process stops.
questions.asked: A design question disguised as a .NET one; the strong answer mentions durability.

questions.q: What does `IHostedService` / `BackgroundService` give you?
choices: A cron-style scheduler that runs a job once across all instances at a set time
A long-running task with startup and graceful-shutdown hooks tied to the host
A durable message queue that keeps pending work safe across process restarts
Automatic retries with exponential backoff for work that fails transiently
questions.why: It gets a CancellationToken on shutdown so it can finish cleanly. It is per instance, though: scale to three replicas and your "nightly job" runs three times unless you add a distributed lock or a real scheduler. It has no queue, schedule or retry logic of its own.
questions.asked: The "it runs on every instance" catch is the part that shows production experience.

questions.q: A request to `/me` carries a valid bearer token. What response does it get?
choices: 200, because endpoint routing puts the two middlewares in the right order
401, because authorisation runs while the user is still anonymous
403, because the user is authenticated too late to pass the policy
None: the host refuses to start with the middlewares in this order
questions.why: UseAuthentication is what reads the token and fills `HttpContext.User`. Placed after UseAuthorization, the policy check sees an anonymous user and challenges, so every protected endpoint returns 401 even with a valid token. Nothing re-orders them and nothing fails at startup, which is why this bug survives until the first real request.
questions.asked: A classic misconfiguration; recognising the symptom is more useful than reciting the AuthN/AuthZ definition.

questions.q: What is a claims-based identity?
choices: A role name stored in the database and checked by `[Authorize(Roles)]` attributes
The signature of the JWT, which policies compare against the signing key
The user as a set of claims (key/value statements) that policies evaluate
The username typed into the login form, kept in session state per request
questions.why: A ClaimsPrincipal carries claims such as sub, email and role, issued by whatever authenticated the user. Roles are just one kind of claim. Policy-based authorization (`RequireClaim`, `RequireAssertion`, custom requirements) scales better than scattering role names through attributes.
questions.asked: Leads into policies, which is how real apps express "only the owner or an admin".

questions.q: Why is `IMemoryCache` not enough once you scale out?
choices: It has a fixed limit of 100 MB per process, which fills up quickly once traffic grows
It is not thread-safe, so concurrent requests across instances corrupt it
It can hold only strings, so every instance must serialise its objects
Each instance has its own copy, so entries diverge and eviction does not spread
questions.why: Three instances, three caches, three possibly different answers, and evicting on one does nothing to the others. A distributed cache (Redis, or HybridCache in .NET 9 over one) gives a shared view at the cost of a network hop. IMemoryCache is thread-safe, stores objects and has no fixed size limit unless you set one.
questions.asked: Scaling questions start here; the invalidation part is what interviewers push on.

questions.q: What does `WebApplicationFactory<T>` enable?
choices: Load tests that start many copies of the app and measure its throughput under traffic
Integration tests that boot the real app in memory and send it real requests
Generated client SDKs for the API, built from the endpoints the app maps
Migrations run against a fresh test database before each test class starts
questions.why: It tests routing, model binding, middleware, filters and serialisation together, which a unit test on a handler misses, and lets you swap services. Pair it with a real database in a container (Testcontainers) or SQLite in-memory; Microsoft discourages the EF InMemory provider for this, because it behaves nothing like a relational database.
questions.asked: Shows you test the HTTP surface, not only classes in isolation.

questions.q: How do you configure CORS correctly in ASP.NET Core?
choices: AllowAnyOrigin together with AllowCredentials, so every client can send cookies
An Access-Control-Allow-Origin header added by hand in each controller action
A named policy with explicit origins, applied with UseCors before the endpoints
Nothing: ASP.NET Core allows cross-origin requests by default for JSON endpoints
questions.why: Credentials require an explicit origin, so the CORS policy builder throws if you combine AllowAnyOrigin with AllowCredentials, before any browser gets involved. UseCors placed after the endpoints never sees the preflight. Hand-written headers miss preflight handling, and nothing is allowed cross-origin by default.
questions.asked: Every SPA-plus-API project hits CORS; the interviewer wants the server-side mechanics.

questions.q: What does `services.AddHttpClient<T>()` solve?
choices: Retries on transient failures, which it adds to every client with no configuration
JSON serialisation of request and response bodies, which HttpClient cannot do on its own
Socket exhaustion and stale DNS from creating a client per call or keeping one forever
Authentication headers, which it copies from the incoming request to every call
questions.why: `new HttpClient()` per request leaks sockets in TIME_WAIT; a static instance with default settings never picks up DNS changes. The factory pools and recycles handlers and gives you a place to add resilience handlers. A static client with `SocketsHttpHandler.PooledConnectionLifetime` set is also a recommended pattern. Retries are opt-in.
questions.asked: A well-known .NET gotcha that shows whether you have debugged a production networking issue.

questions.q: What changes when ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT is Development instead of Production?
choices: Development turns off DI scope validation and HTTPS, which Production always enables
Production turns off logging, so only Development writes any log output
Development shows the developer exception page with stack traces; Production must not
Nothing at runtime: the variable only picks which appsettings file you edit
questions.why: The environment switches on the developer exception page, user secrets and DI scope validation, and selects `appsettings.{Environment}.json`. A stack trace tells an attacker your framework versions, file paths and sometimes connection strings, so getting this variable wrong in production is a real disclosure risk.
questions.asked: Checks you know what a misconfigured environment variable exposes in production.

questions.q: What is the recommended way to return a 404 from a minimal API endpoint?
choices: Throw a KeyNotFoundException, which the framework maps to a 404 response for you
Return `Results.NotFound()` or `TypedResults.NotFound()` from the handler
Return null, which minimal APIs convert into a 404 Not Found response
Call `context.Abort()` so the client treats the resource as unavailable
questions.why: An unhandled exception becomes a 500, not a 404, and a null return is serialised rather than turned into Not Found. `TypedResults` additionally gives a strongly typed return you can assert on in tests and that feeds OpenAPI metadata correctly. `Abort()` drops the connection.
questions.asked: A quick check of minimal API idioms.

questions.q: You add a field to an entity and the API stops returning existing rows correctly. Where do you look first?
choices: Whether the new field's service is registered correctly in the DI container
Whether a migration was created and applied to that environment's database
Whether the CORS policy lets the new field through to the browser client
Whether the JSON serialiser settings still include properties that are null
questions.why: Model and schema drift is the most common EF Core deployment failure: the code expects a column the database does not have. CORS never filters individual fields, and DI has nothing to do with entity properties. The general lesson: schema changes are deployments, and each environment has its own database state.
questions.asked: A realistic debugging prompt; the interviewer wants a hypothesis, not a guess.

questions.q: What does `MapGroup` give you here?
choices: A separate middleware pipeline that runs only for requests under /api/orders
The two endpoints share the /api/orders prefix and the authorisation requirement
A controller class generated at build time from the handlers mapped in the group
A shared concurrency limit, so only one request in the group runs at a time
questions.why: A route group (.NET 7+) applies a prefix and conventions such as authorisation, filters, tags and rate-limit policies to every endpoint mapped on it. It is endpoint metadata, not a separate middleware branch; for that you would use `app.Map` or `UseWhen`. It keeps a minimal API organised without controllers.
questions.asked: The first thing people ask about minimal APIs is how to organise them; route groups are the answer.

questions.q: What can a minimal API endpoint filter see that a middleware cannot?
choices: The raw request body stream, before anything else in the whole app has read from it
Requests that matched no endpoint at all, such as those that end in 404
The response after it has been sent and the connection has been closed
The handler's bound arguments, such as the deserialised DTO, before it runs
questions.why: Endpoint filters run after model binding, around one handler, so they can validate or transform the actual arguments. Middleware runs earlier on the raw HttpContext and sees every request, including ones that match no endpoint. Use middleware for cross-cutting HTTP concerns and filters for per-endpoint logic that needs the typed inputs.
questions.asked: Checks you know the layers in the pipeline and pick the right one for validation or auditing.

questions.q: What does `ValidateOnStart()` add to this registration?
questions.code:
builder.Services.AddOptions<SmtpOptions>()
    .BindConfiguration("Smtp")
    .ValidateDataAnnotations()
    .ValidateOnStart();
choices: It re-validates the options on every request and rejects requests once they are invalid
It validates appsettings.json against a JSON schema as part of the build
An invalid or missing Smtp setting stops the app at startup, not on first use
It reloads the options automatically whenever the configuration file changes
questions.why: Options are validated lazily by default, when something first reads them, which might be the first password-reset email hours after a deploy. `ValidateOnStart` runs the validation while the host starts, so a bad deploy fails immediately and visibly. It has nothing to do with reloading or per-request checks.
questions.asked: Fail-fast configuration is a production-readiness signal interviewers like to hear.

questions.q: Why prefer the second logging call?
questions.code:
logger.LogInformation($"Order {orderId} shipped to {customerId}");
logger.LogInformation("Order {OrderId} shipped to {CustomerId}", orderId, customerId);
choices: The first does not compile, because the Log methods reject interpolated strings
The second encrypts the values, so they cannot leak into plain-text log files
It keeps OrderId and CustomerId as queryable fields, and skips formatting when disabled
The first logs asynchronously on another thread, so it can reorder your log messages
questions.why: A message template sends the template and the values separately, so a structured sink stores OrderId as a field you can filter on, and all "Order shipped" events group together. The interpolated version bakes the values into one unique string and is formatted even when Information is disabled. It compiles fine, which is why analysers (CA2254) flag it.
questions.asked: Structured logging is how production issues get found; this is the most common mistake in .NET logging.

questions.q: With these mappings, what does `/health/live` report while the database is down?
choices: Unhealthy, because every registered check runs on every health endpoint
Degraded, because the db check is tagged for a different endpoint and is only partly run
Healthy: its predicate selects no checks, so it only proves the app responds
A 404, because an endpoint whose predicate matches no check is not mapped
questions.why: The predicate chooses which registered checks an endpoint runs. `_ => false` runs none, so liveness reports Healthy whenever the process can answer HTTP, and a database outage does not get the app restarted. The tagged readiness endpoint runs the db check and reports Unhealthy, so traffic is routed away until it recovers.
questions.asked: Mixing liveness and readiness causes restart loops during outages; the tag mechanics are how you avoid it in .NET.

questions.q: The 101st request in a minute to `/search` is rejected. What status does it get with this setup?
choices: 429 Too Many Requests, with a Retry-After header added automatically
503 Service Unavailable, unless you set RejectionStatusCode to 429
403 Forbidden, because the limiter runs as part of authorisation
None: it waits in a queue until the next window opens, then succeeds
questions.why: The built-in rate limiter (.NET 7+) rejects with 503 by default. Set `options.RejectionStatusCode = 429` and, if you want Retry-After, write it in `OnRejected`. `QueueLimit` defaults to 0, so nothing waits unless you configure a queue. It is independent of authorisation.
questions.asked: A detail you only know from having shipped it; clients that expect 429 break on the default.

questions.q: What is the key difference between output caching (.NET 7+) and the older response caching middleware?
choices: Output caching sets Cache-Control for browsers; response caching stores responses in Redis
Output caching works only for MVC controllers; response caching works only for minimal API endpoints
Output caching stores HTML pages only; response caching stores JSON API responses only
Output caching stores responses on the server by your rules; response caching obeys HTTP headers
questions.why: Response caching follows HTTP caching semantics, so a client sending `Cache-Control: no-cache` bypasses it and your server cache is only as good as the headers. Output caching is a server-side cache configured by policy, with tag-based eviction and resource locking against stampedes, and it ignores client headers. Both work with any endpoint type.
questions.asked: Checks whether you know which cache you are actually configuring, a common source of "caching does nothing" bugs.

questions.q: In `AddJwtBearer`, what does validating the audience (`ValidAudience`) protect against?
choices: A token issued for a different API by the same identity provider being accepted by yours
A token with a forged signature, because the audience value is part of the signing key itself
A token that has expired, because the audience check also covers the token's lifetime
A token replayed from another browser, because the audience binds it to one device
questions.why: One identity provider often issues tokens for many APIs, all signed with the same key. The `aud` claim says which API a token is for, so without the check a token meant for a low-privilege service works against yours. Signature, lifetime and issuer are separate validations (`ValidateIssuerSigningKey`, `ValidateLifetime`, `ValidIssuer`).
questions.asked: Tests whether you understand what each JWT validation parameter is for, not only that defaults exist.

questions.q: Why is this check done in the handler rather than with `[Authorize(Policy = "CanEdit")]`?
choices: Attributes cannot refer to policies that use custom authorisation requirements
The policy needs the loaded document, such as its owner, which only exists here
IAuthorizationService is faster, because it skips the authentication middleware
Forbid() returns 404 here, hiding that the document exists, unlike the attribute
questions.why: Resource-based authorisation passes the resource into the policy so a handler can compare, for example, `doc.OwnerId` with the user's id. An attribute runs before the handler, when the document has not been loaded. Attributes can use custom requirements, and `Forbid()` produces 403 (or the scheme's forbid behaviour), not 404.
questions.asked: "Users can edit only their own records" is in every CRUD app; this is the idiomatic .NET way to express it.

questions.q: In .NET 8+, what does this setup do with an unhandled exception thrown by an endpoint?
choices: Shows the developer exception page in every environment, including Production
Swallows the exception and returns 200 with an empty body to hide the failure
Calls GlobalExceptionHandler.TryHandleAsync, which can write a ProblemDetails reply
Logs it and lets it reach Kestrel, which then closes the connection without any response
questions.why: `IExceptionHandler` implementations are called in registration order by the exception handler middleware; one that returns true has handled it. Otherwise the middleware falls back to a ProblemDetails 500 via `AddProblemDetails`. It replaces the hand-written try/catch middleware most codebases used to have, and it never exposes stack traces unless you write them.
questions.asked: The modern answer to "how do you handle errors globally in ASP.NET Core?".

questions.q: What does `[FromKeyedServices("s3")]` inject here (.NET 8+)?
choices: The last IStorage registered, because the key is used only for diagnostics
Every implementation at once, injected together as an `IEnumerable<IStorage>`
A new S3Storage on every request, because keyed services are always transient
The S3Storage registration, chosen by its key rather than registration order
questions.why: Keyed services let several implementations of one interface coexist and be requested by key, without writing a factory or a wrapper interface. The lifetime is whatever you registered, a singleton here. Registration order never matters for a keyed lookup; it is only a set of unkeyed `AddSingleton<IStorage, ...>` calls where the last one wins, which is the ambiguity keys exist to avoid.
questions.asked: A recent DI feature that replaces a lot of hand-rolled factory code.

questions.q: A singleton service copies `HttpContext` from `IHttpContextAccessor` into a field in its constructor. What goes wrong?
choices: Nothing: the stored field keeps pointing at whichever request is current at the time
The constructor throws, because a singleton cannot receive the accessor
It keeps one request's HttpContext, which is stale or recycled for later requests
Each request gets its own copy of the singleton, doubling memory use
questions.why: The accessor is safe to inject into a singleton, but only when you read `.HttpContext` at the moment you need it. A stored HttpContext belongs to one request; afterwards its objects are reset and reused, so you read another user's data or get ObjectDisposedException. HttpContext is also not thread-safe, so do not share it across parallel work.
questions.asked: Leads to real data-leak bugs between users; interviewers ask it to find people who have debugged one.

questions.q: Behind a reverse proxy that terminates TLS, `Request.Scheme` is http and `RemoteIpAddress` is the proxy's. What fixes it?
choices: UseHttpsRedirection, which rewrites the request scheme to https on every single request
Setting ASPNETCORE_URLS to an https address, so Kestrel reports https
UseHsts, which tells the app that every request arrived over TLS
UseForwardedHeaders, trusting the proxy, to apply X-Forwarded-For and -Proto
questions.why: The proxy passes the original scheme and client IP in X-Forwarded-Proto and X-Forwarded-For; the forwarded headers middleware applies them, but only from proxies you configure as trusted, so clients cannot spoof them. HTTPS redirection alone causes a redirect loop here, because every request looks like http. HSTS only sets a browser header.
questions.asked: Every containerised deployment sits behind a proxy; wrong scheme and IP break redirects, cookies and rate limiting.

questions.q: In a new .NET 9 Web API project, what generates the OpenAPI document?
choices: Swashbuckle's AddSwaggerGen, which the template still includes by default
NSwag, which is compiled into ASP.NET Core itself starting with .NET 9
Nothing: OpenAPI support was removed from ASP.NET Core in .NET 9
Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi, via AddOpenApi and MapOpenApi
questions.why: From .NET 9 the templates use the built-in Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi package: `AddOpenApi()` registers generation and `MapOpenApi()` serves the JSON document. Swashbuckle was removed from the templates, though it still works if you add it. A UI (Swagger UI or Scalar) is a separate choice.
questions.asked: A currency check; tutorials written before .NET 9 still show Swashbuckle.

questions.q: In .NET 8+, a minimal API endpoint binds `[FromForm]` data and the app uses antiforgery. A POST arrives without a token. What happens?
choices: It succeeds, because minimal API endpoints never validate antiforgery tokens
It is rejected, because form-binding endpoints validate the token automatically
It succeeds, provided that the request also carries a valid authentication cookie
It is redirected to the login page, where the client can fetch a fresh token
questions.why: With `AddAntiforgery()` and `UseAntiforgery()`, minimal API endpoints that bind form data require a valid token and reject the request (400) without one; `DisableAntiforgery()` opts an endpoint out. The auth cookie is exactly what a cross-site form would ride on, so it proves nothing. JSON APIs using bearer tokens do not need this.
questions.asked: Checks you know where CSRF protection is automatic in .NET and where it is not.

questions.q: By default, where does each parameter of this minimal API handler bind from?
questions.code:
app.MapPost("/orders/{id:int}",
    (int id, OrderDto body, IOrderService svc, int? page) => Results.Ok());
choices: id from the route, body from JSON, svc from DI, page from the query string
id and page from the query string, body from the form, svc from the route
id from the route, body from the query string, svc and page from headers
All four from the JSON body, matched to its properties by each parameter name
questions.why: Minimal APIs infer sources: a name in the route template binds from the route, a registered service from DI, a complex type from the JSON body, and remaining simple types from the query string. Use `[FromQuery]`, `[FromHeader]`, `[FromServices]` or `[FromForm]` when the inference is not what you want.
questions.asked: Binding surprises cause most "my parameter is null" questions; knowing the rules prevents them.

questions.q: A minimal API returns `new { Status = OrderStatus.Shipped }` and the React client receives `{"status": 2}`. Why, and what is the idiomatic fix?
choices: System.Text.Json writes enums as numbers by default; add `JsonStringEnumConverter` to the JSON options
Web defaults camel-cased the property and dropped its enum type; decorate it with `[JsonPropertyName]`
The anonymous type boxed the enum to an int; return a record with a typed `OrderStatus` property instead
The client sent `Accept: application/json` without a schema; add OpenAPI so it can map the number back
questions.why: System.Text.Json serialises an enum as its underlying integer unless a converter says otherwise; `builder.Services.ConfigureHttpJsonOptions(o => o.SerializerOptions.Converters.Add(new JsonStringEnumConverter()))` (or `AddJsonOptions` for controllers) makes it write and accept "Shipped". Camel-casing only touches the property name, an anonymous type keeps the enum's type, and OpenAPI describes output rather than changing it. Numbers also break the moment someone reorders the enum.
questions.asked: A first-week bug on every .NET-plus-React team; the interviewer wants the mechanism and the one-line fix.

questions.q: Both lines run in Program.cs. What does a constructor that takes a single `INotifier` receive?
questions.code:
builder.Services.AddScoped<INotifier, EmailNotifier>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<INotifier, SmsNotifier>();
choices: An `EmailNotifier`, because the first registration for a service type wins
An `SmsNotifier`, because the last registration wins for a single resolve
Nothing: the host throws at startup because `INotifier` is registered twice
A composite that forwards each call to both notifiers in registration order
questions.why: The default container keeps every registration; resolving one `INotifier` gives the last, and injecting `IEnumerable<INotifier>` gives both in order. It never throws on duplicates and never builds a composite for you, which is why accidental double registration fails silently.
questions.asked: Tests whether you know how plug-in style registrations work and why a library registration can silently override yours.

questions.q: A reusable library registers its default `IClock` in an `AddMyLibrary()` extension. Why should it use `TryAddSingleton` rather than `AddSingleton`?
choices: `TryAddSingleton` skips the registration if the app has already registered an `IClock`
`TryAddSingleton` catches exceptions thrown by the constructor and falls back to null
`TryAddSingleton` makes the registration thread-safe when several hosts start together
`TryAddSingleton` delays creating the instance until the first request has arrived
questions.why: The `TryAdd*` methods (in `Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection.Extensions`) add only when no registration for the service type exists, so an app that registered its own `IClock` first keeps it. Every singleton is created lazily on first resolve anyway, so that is not what TryAdd adds.
questions.asked: Separates people who have written reusable registration code from people who have only consumed it.

questions.q: What is the difference between `sp.GetService<IFoo>()` and `sp.GetRequiredService<IFoo>()` when `IFoo` is not registered?
choices: `GetService` throws `InvalidOperationException`; `GetRequiredService` returns null
Each returns null; `GetRequiredService` also logs a warning at startup
`GetService` returns null; `GetRequiredService` throws `InvalidOperationException`
Each throws, but only `GetRequiredService` names the missing type
questions.why: `GetService` is the optional lookup and returns null for an unregistered type, which usually surfaces later as a confusing `NullReferenceException`. `GetRequiredService` fails immediately with a message naming the type. Prefer constructor injection; when you must resolve manually, prefer the required form.
questions.asked: A quick check that you fail fast instead of passing nulls around.

questions.q: In Program.cs, what happens when this line runs after `var app = builder.Build();`?
questions.code: builder.Services.AddScoped<IReportService, ReportService>();
choices: It works, but only requests that start after this line can resolve the service
It registers the service as a singleton, since the scope factory is already built
It is ignored silently, so resolving `IReportService` later returns null
It throws `InvalidOperationException`: the service collection is now read-only
questions.why: `Build()` creates the service provider from the collection and makes the collection read-only, so any later `Add*` throws. All registrations belong before `Build()`. A silently ignored registration would be worse, which is why the framework throws instead.
questions.asked: A first-week mistake when moving code around in Program.cs; the interviewer wants to hear that Build freezes the container.

questions.q: A service depends on a type nobody registered. With the default `WebApplication` host, when does the error appear?
choices: At startup in every environment, because the container validates on build
At startup in Development; in Production only on the first resolve
Only when the service is first resolved, whichever environment the app runs in
Never as an error: the missing dependency is injected as null and fails later
questions.why: In Development the host turns on `ValidateOnBuild` and `ValidateScopes`, so building the provider checks every registration's constructor. In other environments both are off by default for startup speed, so the failure waits for the first resolve. You can switch them on everywhere via `builder.Host.UseDefaultServiceProvider`.
questions.asked: Explains the classic 'works on my machine, 500s in production on one endpoint' report and shows you know the dev-only validation.

questions.q: What does this registration let you inject?
questions.code: builder.Services.AddScoped(typeof(IRepository<>), typeof(EfRepository<>));
choices: `IRepository<T>` for any `T`, each closed over the matching `EfRepository<T>`
Only the non-generic `IRepository`, since `typeof` erases the type arguments
One shared `EfRepository<object>` that is cast to whichever `T` is requested
Nothing until each closed type such as `IRepository<Order>` is also registered
questions.why: This is an open generic registration: when something asks for `IRepository<Order>`, the container closes `EfRepository<>` over `Order` and creates it with the registered lifetime. No per-type registration is needed, and nothing is shared across different `T`.
questions.asked: Common in codebases with a generic repository or pipeline behaviours; the interviewer checks you can read the registration.

questions.q: Which of these singletons will the container dispose when the app shuts down?
choices: All three, because every registered singleton is owned by the root provider
Only `CacheC`, because it is the only instance the container can see up front
`CacheA` and `CacheB`; `CacheC` was created by you, so you must dispose it
None of them: singletons live until the process exits and are never disposed
questions.why: The container disposes what it creates, including instances returned from a factory. An instance you construct and pass in is treated as owned by you, so its `Dispose` is not called. This matters for anything holding sockets or file handles.
questions.asked: A subtle ownership rule that shows up when a registered client leaks connections on shutdown.

questions.q: A singleton creates a scope to use a service that implements only `IAsyncDisposable`. Why use `CreateAsyncScope` here?
choices: `CreateScope` runs every resolved service on a single thread, which deadlocks here
`CreateAsyncScope` resolves services in parallel, which makes startup faster
`CreateScope` shares the singleton's scope, so `Exporter` would never be disposed
Disposing a sync scope that holds an async-only disposable throws at runtime
questions.why: A scope disposed with `Dispose()` cannot call `DisposeAsync`, so the container throws `InvalidOperationException` for a service that implements only `IAsyncDisposable`. `CreateAsyncScope` returns an `AsyncServiceScope` you can `await using`. Neither method changes threading or resolution order.
questions.asked: Checks that you have created scopes by hand in hosted services and hit the async disposal rule.

questions.q: In C# 12, what is the main caveat of injecting through a primary constructor like this?
choices: The container cannot see primary constructors, so it needs `[ActivatorUtilitiesConstructor]`
The captured parameters are mutable, not `readonly` fields, so code can reassign them
Primary constructor parameters are copied per call, so each method gets a new repository
A class with a primary constructor must be registered as a singleton in the container
questions.why: The container sees a primary constructor like any other constructor. The parameters are captured into compiler-generated state that code in the class can reassign, which a `private readonly` field would forbid. Some teams assign them to readonly fields or rely on an analyser for that reason.
questions.asked: Primary constructors are now everywhere in .NET 8+ code; a strong answer knows the readonly trade-off.

questions.q: What is the difference between `app.Use(...)` and `app.Run(...)`?
choices: `Use` runs before routing and `Run` after it, whatever order they are written in
`Use` adds middleware that can call the next one; `Run` adds a terminal delegate
`Use` is for synchronous middleware and `Run` for middleware that awaits I/O
`Use` applies to every request and `Run` only to requests matching an endpoint
questions.why: `Use` receives the next delegate and decides whether to call it. `Run` receives only the `HttpContext`, so nothing registered after it on that branch ever executes. Both run in registration order and both can be async.
questions.asked: A warm-up that confirms you understand the pipeline is a chain of delegates.

questions.q: A request arrives for `/admin/users`. What do `Request.PathBase` and `Request.Path` hold inside this branch?
choices: PathBase is empty and Path is `/admin/users`, since Map does not alter the request
PathBase is `/admin/users` and Path is empty, because the whole path was matched
PathBase is `/admin` and Path is `/users`: Map moves the matched segment across
PathBase is `/` and Path is `/admin/users`, because PathBase is always the site root
questions.why: `Map` branches on a path prefix and moves the matched segment from `Path` to `PathBase`, so the branch sees paths relative to its mount point. A branch created with `Map` never rejoins the main pipeline, which is the other thing people forget.
questions.asked: Branching is how health or admin sub-apps get mounted; the PathBase detail explains many broken redirects.

questions.q: What is the practical difference between `app.UseWhen(pred, branch)` and `app.MapWhen(pred, branch)`?
choices: `UseWhen` rejoins the main pipeline after the branch; `MapWhen` never does
`UseWhen` tests the path only; `MapWhen` can test any part of the request
`UseWhen` runs the branch after the endpoint; `MapWhen` runs it before routing
`UseWhen` evaluates the predicate once at startup; `MapWhen` does so per request
questions.why: Both take a predicate over `HttpContext` evaluated per request. With `UseWhen`, if the branch does not short-circuit, the request continues into the rest of the main pipeline. `MapWhen` forks permanently, so the branch must end in something that writes a response.
questions.asked: Asked when someone wants extra middleware only for `/api` paths; picking the wrong one silently drops requests.

questions.q: This middleware sometimes throws 'Headers are read-only, response has already started'. What is the fix?
choices: Set the header before `await next(ctx)` and keep updating it as the request runs
Wrap the header assignment in a try/catch so the error is logged and ignored
Call `ctx.Response.Clear()` after `next` so the headers become writable again
Set it in a `ctx.Response.OnStarting` callback registered before `next`
questions.why: Once the endpoint writes to the body, the headers have been sent and are read-only, so code after `next` cannot add one. `OnStarting` runs just before the headers go out. `Clear` throws once the response has started, and a value set before `next` cannot be the elapsed time.
questions.asked: Tests whether you understand that a response streams out, which explains a whole class of middleware bugs.

questions.q: A convention-based middleware class takes `AppDbContext` in its constructor. What goes wrong?
choices: Nothing: middleware constructors are called once per request, like controllers
The middleware is built once for the app, so one DbContext serves every request
The host refuses to start, because middleware cannot have constructor parameters
Each request gets a new DbContext, but it is never disposed after the request
questions.why: Convention-based middleware is instantiated once when the pipeline is built, so a scoped dependency in its constructor is captured for the app's lifetime. Take scoped services as extra parameters of `InvokeAsync`, which are resolved per request, or implement `IMiddleware`.
questions.asked: The captive-dependency bug in its most common real form; interviewers like it because it looks harmless.

questions.q: How does a middleware that implements `IMiddleware` differ from a convention-based one?
choices: It is resolved from DI for each request, so it must be registered and may be scoped
It can only be used in minimal APIs, since controllers expect convention middleware
It runs outside the pipeline on a background thread, after the response is sent
It is created once at startup, which makes it the faster choice for hot paths
questions.why: `UseMiddleware<T>()` with an `IMiddleware` type asks `IMiddlewareFactory` to resolve it per request, so you must register it (for example `AddScoped<MyMiddleware>()`), and its constructor can take scoped services. Convention-based middleware is the one created once at startup.
questions.asked: Follows the captive-dependency question: the interviewer wants the alternative and its registration requirement.

questions.q: Why does `app.UseExceptionHandler(...)` normally go first in the pipeline?
choices: It must run before routing, or endpoints cannot be matched for error paths
It only catches exceptions thrown by middleware registered before it runs
It wraps everything registered after it, so it sees their exceptions
The framework requires it first and throws at startup if it is placed later
questions.why: Each middleware wraps the ones added after it, so an exception handler added first sees failures from the whole pipeline. Placed after, say, authentication, it cannot catch what authentication throws. Nothing validates the position at startup; it just silently catches less.
questions.asked: A direct application of 'order matters' that shows you can reason about the pipeline rather than recite it.

questions.q: In .NET 8+, you register two `IExceptionHandler` implementations. What does returning `false` from `TryHandleAsync` do?
choices: It rethrows the exception so the server returns an empty 500 immediately
It hands the exception to the next handler in registration order
It marks the exception as handled but leaves the response for the endpoint
It retries the request once, then hands the exception to the next handler
questions.why: Handlers run in the order they were registered, and returning `true` stops the chain. If every handler returns `false`, the middleware falls back to its default behaviour, which with `AddProblemDetails` writes a ProblemDetails 500. Nothing is retried.
questions.asked: The modern replacement for hand-written try/catch middleware; interviewers check you know the chain semantics.

questions.q: In a .NET 8+ app built with `WebApplication.CreateBuilder`, how is the developer exception page enabled?
choices: It is always on and must be turned off manually before deploying to production
You must call `app.UseDeveloperExceptionPage()` yourself in every environment
It is only available to controllers, not to minimal API endpoints
The host adds it automatically when the environment is Development
questions.why: `WebApplication` adds the developer exception page for you when `IsDevelopment()` is true, so stack traces never leak in Production by default. Calling it manually is legacy template code, and it covers every endpoint type.
questions.asked: Checks that you know what the minimal hosting model does implicitly, which matters when a stack trace shows up in the wrong place.

questions.q: Why do the templates call `app.UseHsts()` only outside Development?
choices: Browsers remember HSTS per host, forcing HTTPS on every localhost app
HSTS needs a certificate from a public CA, and dev certificates are self-signed
Kestrel cannot send the header over HTTP/2, which is what dev servers use
The header slows hot reload, because every change needs a new TLS handshake
questions.why: `Strict-Transport-Security` tells the browser to use HTTPS for that host for `max-age`, and browsers remember it. On localhost that breaks every other project you run over plain HTTP. The certificate type and HTTP version are irrelevant to the decision.
questions.asked: Shows you know what HSTS does in the browser rather than treating it as a magic security switch.

questions.q: With this endpoint, what does `GET /orders/abc` return?
questions.code: app.MapGet("/orders/{id:int}", (int id) => TypedResults.Ok(id));
choices: 400 Bad Request, because `abc` cannot be converted to the `int` parameter
404 Not Found, because the `int` route constraint means no endpoint matches
422 Unprocessable Content with a ProblemDetails body naming the `id` field
200 OK with `0`, because a failed conversion leaves the default value
questions.why: Route constraints take part in matching: `abc` fails `:int`, so the route is not a candidate and routing yields 404. Without the constraint the route would match and parameter binding would fail with 400. Constraints are for disambiguating routes, not for input validation.
questions.asked: Tests the distinction between routing and binding, which explains why clients see 404 instead of a helpful 400.

questions.q: Both endpoints are mapped. Which one handles `GET /items/new`?
questions.code:
app.MapGet("/items/{id}", (string id) => $"item {id}");
app.MapGet("/items/new", () => "new form");
choices: `/items/{id}`, because it was registered first and routes match in order
Neither: two matching templates cause an ambiguous match error
`/items/new`, because literal segments outrank route parameters
Whichever the router picks at random, so the result changes between runs
questions.why: Endpoint routing orders candidates by template precedence, not registration order: literal segments beat parameters, and constrained parameters beat unconstrained ones. Ambiguity only arises when two templates have equal precedence and both match.
questions.asked: Explains routing behaviour people otherwise learn from bugs, and contrasts with order-sensitive routers like Express.

questions.q: Two controllers accidentally declare `[HttpGet("api/reports")]`. What happens when a client calls that URL?
choices: The first controller alphabetically handles it; the other is skipped
The app fails at startup with a duplicate route error listing both actions
Each action runs in turn and the results are merged into one array
The request fails with an ambiguous match exception, which becomes a 500
questions.why: Routing detects the ambiguity only when a request matches both endpoints with equal precedence, and throws `AmbiguousMatchException`, which surfaces as a 500. Startup does not validate route uniqueness, so the bug ships unless a test calls the URL.
questions.asked: A real merge-conflict bug; the interviewer wants to hear that it is a runtime failure and how a test would catch it.

questions.q: A custom middleware reads `context.GetEndpoint()?.Metadata` to find an attribute. Where must it be placed to see a non-null endpoint?
choices: Before `UseRouting`, because routing clears the endpoint once it has matched
After routing has run, since routing is what selects the endpoint
Anywhere, because the endpoint is chosen when the request is first accepted
Only inside an endpoint filter; middleware can never see endpoint metadata
questions.why: Routing matches the request and stores the chosen endpoint on the context; the endpoint runs later at the end of the pipeline. Middleware between the two, such as authorization, CORS and rate limiting, can read its metadata. `WebApplication` inserts `UseRouting` at the start if you do not call it, so explicit placement only matters when you do.
questions.asked: This is how authorization knows about `[Authorize]`; explaining it shows you understand endpoint routing's two halves.

questions.q: What does `.ShortCircuit()` (.NET 8+) do to this endpoint?
questions.code:
app.MapGet("/robots.txt", () => "User-agent: *
Disallow:").ShortCircuit();
choices: It caches the response in memory so later requests skip the handler
It runs the handler before `UseExceptionHandler`, so errors are not caught
It runs the endpoint straight after routing, skipping later middleware
It returns 204 to HEAD requests without running the handler at all
questions.why: A short-circuited endpoint executes as soon as routing matches it, so middleware such as authentication, authorization and CORS never runs for it. It suits cheap, public responses like robots.txt or health pings. Nothing is cached, and middleware placed before routing still runs.
questions.asked: A .NET 8 addition interviewers use to check you know which middleware sits after routing.

questions.q: In a minimal API, what does this handler send?
choices: 201 with a `Location` header for the new order and the order as JSON
200 with the order as JSON, plus a `Content-Location` header
201 with an empty body, since a Created result never writes the resource
302 redirecting the client to `/orders/{id}` so it can fetch the order
questions.why: `Created` sets status 201, puts the URI in `Location` and serialises the value as the body. A redirect would force a second round trip, and `Content-Location` means something different in RFC 9110.
questions.asked: The basic 'what should a POST return' check, asked in ASP.NET terms.

questions.q: Why do many teams prefer `TypedResults.Ok(order)` over `Results.Ok(order)` in minimal APIs?
choices: `TypedResults` serialises faster because it uses source-generated JSON
`Results` is obsolete in .NET 9 and produces a compiler warning
`TypedResults` writes the status code before the body starts streaming
`TypedResults` returns concrete types that OpenAPI and tests can read
questions.why: `Results.Ok` returns `IResult`, which says nothing about the response. `TypedResults.Ok` returns `Ok<Order>`, so the framework can describe the 200 response in OpenAPI and a unit test can check the type and value directly. Both serialise the same way, and `Results` is not obsolete.
questions.asked: Shows you have written tested, documented minimal APIs rather than demos.

questions.q: Why does this handler declare `Results<Ok<Order>, NotFound>` as its return type?
questions.code:
app.MapGet("/orders/{id}", async Task<Results<Ok<Order>, NotFound>> (int id, IOrderRepo repo) =>
    await repo.Find(id) is { } o ? TypedResults.Ok(o) : TypedResults.NotFound());
choices: Without it the lambda's two branches have no common type, and OpenAPI loses both
It tells the runtime to try `Ok` first and fall back to `NotFound` on an exception
It is needed only for AOT, because reflection cannot inspect lambda return types
It makes the endpoint return 404 automatically whenever the handler returns null
questions.why: `Ok<Order>` and `NotFound` are different types, so the conditional has no natural type; the `Results<...>` union gives it one and implicitly converts from each. The union also tells the OpenAPI generator both possible responses. It changes nothing about null handling or exceptions.
questions.asked: Tests whether you have hit the compiler error and understand the union type rather than falling back to `IResult`.

questions.q: What does each of these minimal API endpoints send back?
questions.code:
app.MapGet("/a", () => "hello");
app.MapGet("/b", () => new { Message = "hello" });
choices: Each sends JSON: `/a` sends a quoted string and `/b` an object
`/a` sends `text/plain` `hello`; `/b` sends JSON `{"message":"hello"}`
`/a` sends `text/html`; `/b` sends JSON with the property kept as `Message`
Each sends `text/plain`, because neither handler returns `IResult`
questions.why: Minimal APIs write a returned `string` as `text/plain` and serialise any other object as JSON using the web defaults, which camel-case property names. Return `TypedResults.Json(...)` if you really want a JSON string.
questions.asked: A small surprise that breaks clients expecting JSON everywhere.

questions.q: In what order do these endpoint filters run around the handler?
choices: `ValidationFilter` first, because the last filter added is the outermost
In parallel, and the handler runs after whichever one finishes last
`AuditFilter` outermost, then `ValidationFilter`, then the handler
In alphabetical order of the filter type names, whatever order they are added
questions.why: Endpoint filters form a pipeline like middleware: the first one added is outermost, so its code before `next` runs first and its code after `next` runs last. Put a validation filter where you want invalid requests to stop, and remember outer filters still see the short-circuited result.
questions.asked: Checks whether you can reason about filter pipelines the same way you reason about middleware.

questions.q: In a controller, what is the difference between returning `ActionResult<Order>` and `IActionResult`?
choices: `ActionResult<Order>` always returns 200; `IActionResult` can return any status
`IActionResult` is for synchronous actions; `ActionResult<T>` is for async ones
`ActionResult<Order>` returns the entity untracked; `IActionResult` keeps tracking
`ActionResult<Order>` lets you return an `Order` directly and documents its type
questions.why: `ActionResult<T>` has implicit conversions from both `T` and `ActionResult`, so `return order;` and `return NotFound();` both compile, and OpenAPI knows the success body type. `IActionResult` hides the type unless you add `[ProducesResponseType]`. Neither relates to sync versus async or to EF tracking.
questions.asked: A controllers basic that also checks whether you think about API documentation.

questions.q: In a controller with `[ApiController]`, where does a complex-type parameter like `CreateOrder cmd` bind from if it has no attribute?
choices: The query string, with each property read from a matching query key
The request body, because complex types are inferred as `[FromBody]`
The form, because `[ApiController]` assumes HTML form posts by default
Route values first, then the query string, then the body, in that order
questions.why: `[ApiController]` applies binding source inference: complex types come from the body, parameters named in the route template from the route, services from DI, and remaining simple types from the query. Without `[ApiController]` complex types are bound from form, route and query values instead, which is why a JSON body can arrive empty.
questions.asked: Explains the classic 'my JSON body is always empty' bug in controllers without the attribute.

questions.q: You want a controller to return your own error shape instead of the automatic 400 that `[ApiController]` sends for invalid models. What is the supported hook?
choices: Replace `ApiBehaviorOptions.InvalidModelStateResponseFactory`
Throw a `ValidationException` from the action and catch it in exception middleware
Remove `[ApiController]` and check `ModelState.IsValid` at the top of each action
Register a `JsonConverter` for `ModelStateDictionary` so it serialises differently
questions.why: The automatic 400 comes from a filter that calls `InvalidModelStateResponseFactory`, so replacing that delegate changes the response everywhere. The action never runs when the model is invalid, so throwing from it is too late. Dropping `[ApiController]` loses inference and attribute-routing checks too.
questions.asked: Asked on teams with a house error format; it shows you know where the automatic behaviour lives.

questions.q: In what order do MVC filter types run for a controller action that passes authorization?
choices: Action, authorization, resource, then result filters, with exception filters last
Resource, authorization, action, result, all in the order they were registered
Authorization, resource, action around the action, then result
Exception filters first, so they can wrap all the others in one try/catch block
questions.why: Authorization filters run first and can short-circuit; resource filters wrap most of the rest, including model binding; action filters wrap the action; result filters wrap writing the result. Exception filters handle exceptions from the action and action filters, not from the whole pipeline.
questions.asked: Shows depth with MVC, and matters when deciding whether a cross-cutting concern belongs in a filter or middleware.

questions.q: A filter needs `IAuditStore` from DI. Why use `[ServiceFilter(typeof(AuditFilter))]` rather than `[AuditFilter]`?
choices: Attributes are built by reflection, so they cannot take DI services
`[ServiceFilter]` runs the filter on every action, while an attribute runs it once
An attribute filter cannot short-circuit, while a service filter can set a result
`[ServiceFilter]` runs the filter asynchronously; attribute filters run synchronously
questions.why: Attribute arguments must be compile-time constants and the attribute is created by reflection, so constructor injection is impossible. `ServiceFilter` resolves the filter from DI, so it must be registered; `TypeFilter` creates it with `ActivatorUtilities` without registration. Both kinds can short-circuit and be async.
questions.asked: A classic MVC question; it checks you understand attribute limitations rather than memorising names.

questions.q: In .NET 9, what happens when the app maps this minimal API endpoint?
questions.code: app.MapPost("/transfer", (Account from, Account to) => Transfer(from, to));
choices: Each parameter reads its own top-level property, `from` and `to`, of the JSON body
The body is deserialised twice, once into each parameter, so both hold the same data
Building the endpoint throws: only one parameter may be inferred from the body
`from` is bound from the body and `to` from the query string, in declaration order
questions.why: A request has one body stream, so minimal APIs allow a single body parameter and fail with an `InvalidOperationException` listing the inferred body parameters. Wrap both in one request DTO. There is no per-property splitting of the body and no fallback to the query string for complex types.
questions.asked: A common first error with minimal APIs; the fix (one request DTO) is the answer the interviewer wants.

questions.q: In .NET 9 this GET endpoint throws an `InvalidOperationException` instead of running. What is the idiomatic fix?
questions.code:
record SearchFilter(string? Term, int Page, int PageSize);
app.MapGet("/products", (SearchFilter filter, CatalogDb db) => Search(db, filter));
choices: Add `[FromBody]` to `filter` so the GET request's JSON body is read explicitly
Add `[AsParameters]` so each property of `SearchFilter` binds from the query
Register `SearchFilter` in DI so the container can construct it for each request
Change the verb to `MapPost`, because GET endpoints cannot take complex types
questions.why: Minimal APIs do not infer a body for GET, so a complex parameter with no source cannot be bound. `[AsParameters]` binds each constructor parameter or property by the normal rules, here from the query string. A GET body is technically allowed but ignored by many proxies and clients, and switching verbs breaks caching.
questions.asked: Search and filter endpoints are everywhere in CRUD apps; `[AsParameters]` is the tidy answer.

questions.q: How does a minimal API bind a query value to a custom type like `Point` in `/nearby?at=51.5,-0.12`?
choices: Give `Point` a static `TryParse(string?, out Point)` method to parse the value
Register a `JsonConverter<Point>`, because query values are parsed as JSON by default
Add a `TypeConverter` attribute to `Point`, which minimal APIs look up via reflection
It cannot: minimal APIs bind only primitives from the query and need a DTO body
questions.why: Minimal APIs look for a static `TryParse` (or `BindAsync(HttpContext, ParameterInfo)` for full control) on the parameter type and use it for route, query and header values. JSON converters apply only to bodies, and `TypeConverter` is an MVC model-binding mechanism.
questions.asked: Shows you know the extension points instead of parsing strings by hand in every handler.

questions.q: What does `ids` contain for `GET /orders?ids=3&ids=7` in .NET 8+?
questions.code: app.MapGet("/orders", (int[] ids) => ids);
choices: Only `[7]`, because the last value of a repeated query key wins
Only `[3]`, because binding stops at the first matching key
Nothing: arrays bind from the JSON body, so this request gets a 400
`[3, 7]`, as arrays bind every value of a repeated key
questions.why: Since .NET 7, array and `StringValues` parameters of simple types bind from repeated query keys (and headers). For GET this is inferred without an attribute. The first-or-last-wins behaviour applies only when binding a single value.
questions.asked: Filter-by-several-ids is a common endpoint, and knowing the repeated-key convention avoids comma-splitting code.

questions.q: Why is this handler given a `CancellationToken` parameter?
questions.code:
app.MapGet("/report", async (ReportService svc, CancellationToken ct) =>
    TypedResults.Ok(await svc.BuildAsync(ct)));
choices: It binds to `RequestAborted`, so work stops when the client disconnects
It enforces the default 30-second request timeout configured in Kestrel
It is required for every async handler, or the endpoint runs synchronously
It lets the framework cancel the handler when the app pool recycles hourly
questions.why: `CancellationToken` is a special parameter type bound to `RequestAborted`, which fires when the client goes away. Passing it down to EF Core or HttpClient calls stops wasted work. It is optional, and Kestrel has no default request-processing timeout for it to enforce.
questions.asked: Checks that you propagate cancellation, a cheap habit that interviewers read as production experience.

questions.q: Each endpoint is called with no query string. What does each one do?
questions.code:
app.MapGet("/a", (int page) => page);
app.MapGet("/b", (int page = 1) => page);
choices: `/a` returns 0 and `/b` returns 1, since missing values use the default
`/a` returns 400 because `page` is required; `/b` returns 1
Each returns 400, because a query value is required for any `int`
`/a` throws a `NullReferenceException`, which becomes a 500
questions.why: Minimal APIs treat a non-nullable parameter without a default as required and reject the request with 400 when it is missing. Make it optional with `int?` or a default value. The value type never silently becomes 0.
questions.asked: A quick check of how optionality is expressed in minimal APIs, which drives the OpenAPI document too.

questions.q: A client posts `{"Name":"Tea","PRICE":3}` to a minimal API bound to `record Product(string Name, decimal Price)`. What does the handler get?
choices: `Name` is bound but `Price` stays 0, since only exact camelCase keys match
Nothing: the request is rejected with 400 because the casing does not match
`Name = "Tea"`, `Price = 3`: the web defaults read case-insensitively
`Name` and `Price` both stay default, since PascalCase keys are ignored
questions.why: ASP.NET Core uses `JsonSerializerDefaults.Web`: camelCase on write and case-insensitive property matching on read. A console app calling `JsonSerializer.Deserialize` without options is case-sensitive, which is where the 'it works in the API but not in my test' confusion comes from.
questions.asked: Explains why the same JSON binds in the API but not in a unit test using default serializer options.

questions.q: A client sends `{"quantity": "5"}` for an `int Quantity` property in an ASP.NET Core API. What happens?
choices: The request fails with 400, since a JSON string is never converted to a number
Quantity stays 0 and a warning is written to the log for the property
The value is parsed only when the property is marked with `[JsonNumber]`
Quantity is 5: the web defaults allow reading numbers from JSON strings
questions.why: `JsonSerializerDefaults.Web` sets `NumberHandling = AllowReadingFromString`, so quoted numbers are accepted. Plain `JsonSerializer` defaults are strict and would throw. If you want the strict behaviour in the API you configure it explicitly.
questions.asked: A detail that surprises people comparing API behaviour with unit tests; knowing it shows you have read the defaults.

questions.q: A client adds `"isAdmin": true` to a JSON body whose DTO has no `IsAdmin` property. With default System.Text.Json settings, what happens to that key?
choices: It is ignored: unknown properties are skipped unless you opt out
It is rejected: unknown properties make the request fail with a 400
It is stored in `HttpContext.Items` so middleware can inspect it later on
It is bound to any property with a similar name, such as `Admin`
questions.why: Unmapped JSON members are skipped by default, which is why a DTO without the property is the real defence against overposting. .NET 8 added `JsonUnmappedMemberHandling.Disallow` if you want strict contracts. Nothing does fuzzy name matching.
questions.asked: Connects serialisation defaults to overposting, a real security review topic.

questions.q: You add `JsonStringEnumConverter` with `builder.Services.ConfigureHttpJsonOptions(...)`, but a controller still returns enums as numbers. Why?
choices: Enums are always serialised as numbers in controllers for compatibility
The converter must also be registered as a singleton in the container
`ConfigureHttpJsonOptions` must run after `builder.Build()` to take effect
It configures minimal APIs; controllers use `AddJsonOptions`
questions.why: Minimal APIs and MVC keep separate `JsonOptions` types, configured by `ConfigureHttpJsonOptions` and `AddJsonOptions` respectively. An app that mixes both styles must configure both. Configuration after `Build()` would throw rather than apply.
questions.asked: A real mixed-codebase bug; the answer shows you know the two stacks are configured separately.

questions.q: An endpoint returns EF Core entities where `Order.Customer.Orders` points back at the order. What does System.Text.Json do by default?
choices: It serialises each object once and writes `null` wherever a cycle appears
It follows the cycle forever until the process runs out of stack space
It throws `JsonException` because a possible object cycle was detected
It writes `$ref` pointers that JavaScript clients resolve automatically
questions.why: The default has no cycle handling and throws when it passes the maximum depth, reporting a possible cycle. `ReferenceHandler.IgnoreCycles` writes null and `Preserve` writes `$id`/`$ref`, but the better fix is to return DTOs rather than tracked entity graphs.
questions.asked: Returning entities from endpoints is a code-review smell; the interviewer wants DTOs, not a serializer flag.

questions.q: What does System.Text.Json (.NET 8+) do when the JSON omits `Email` for this type?
choices: It sets `Email` to an empty string, because `required` only affects `new` calls
It throws `JsonException`, because `required` members must be present in JSON
It sets `Email` to null and logs a nullable warning at runtime
It skips the object and returns null from `Deserialize` without an error
questions.why: Since .NET 7 System.Text.Json honours the C# `required` modifier (and `[JsonRequired]`), so a missing property fails deserialisation; in an API that becomes a 400. It checks presence only: an explicit `"email": null` still gets through unless you also enable nullable-annotation checks.
questions.asked: Shows you know which contract checks happen in the serializer versus in validation.

questions.q: In .NET 9, a client sends `"name": null` for a non-nullable `string Name` property. What does System.Text.Json do by default?
choices: It rejects the payload, because nullable annotations are enforced by default
It substitutes an empty string so the non-nullable contract still holds
It stores null; enforcement needs `RespectNullableAnnotations`
It leaves `Name` at its initialiser's value and ignores the null silently
questions.why: Nullable reference types are compile-time only, so by default the serializer happily writes null into a `string`. .NET 9 added `JsonSerializerOptions.RespectNullableAnnotations`, off by default, to make it throw instead. Validation attributes are the other guard.
questions.asked: Probes whether you know NRT annotations are not runtime checks, a frequent source of null bugs.

questions.q: In .NET 9, a minimal API takes `CreateUser` with `[Required]` and `[EmailAddress]` attributes. What checks them?
choices: Nothing: .NET 9 minimal APIs do not run DataAnnotations validation
The JSON serializer, which reads validation attributes while deserialising
The routing middleware, which returns 400 before the endpoint is selected
The `[ApiController]` filter, which minimal APIs apply to every endpoint
questions.why: Up to .NET 9, minimal APIs ignore DataAnnotations; you validate with a library, a filter or by hand. .NET 10 adds built-in support you switch on with `builder.Services.AddValidation()`, which returns a validation ProblemDetails 400. `[ApiController]` is an MVC feature only.
questions.asked: Teams moving from controllers get caught by this; the .NET 10 change is the up-to-date part of the answer.

questions.q: Why does `[Required]` never fail for this property in a model bound from JSON?
choices: `[Required]` works only on strings; numbers need `[MinLength]` instead
A missing `int` defaults to 0, which is a value, so `[Required]` passes
Validation attributes apply only to route and query values, not to bodies
`[Required]` runs before deserialisation, when the property is always set
questions.why: `[Required]` checks for null, and a value type is never null, so an absent `Quantity` arrives as 0 and passes. Make it `int?` with `[Required]` to detect absence, or use `[Range(1, 100)]` to reject 0. `[MinLength]` is for strings and collections.
questions.asked: A classic validation bug that separates people who have tested their validation from those who assumed it worked.

questions.q: In an `[ApiController]` with nullable reference types enabled, a client omits `Title` for `public string Title { get; set; }`. What happens?
choices: Title is null and the action runs, since NRT is only a compile-time feature
Title becomes an empty string, because non-nullable strings get a default
The JSON serializer throws, which the framework turns into a 500 response
MVC treats the non-nullable property as required, so the client gets a 400
questions.why: MVC infers an implicit `[Required]` for non-nullable reference-type properties and parameters, so the automatic 400 fires. This is controlled by `SuppressImplicitRequiredAttributeForNonNullableReferenceTypes`. The serializer itself does not enforce annotations, which is why the other stack differs.
questions.asked: Explains surprising 400s after a team turns on nullable reference types.

questions.q: A booking DTO must reject `EndDate` earlier than `StartDate`. Which DataAnnotations-friendly mechanism fits?
choices: Put `[Range]` on `EndDate` with `StartDate` passed as the attribute's minimum
Implement `IValidatableObject` and return a result from its `Validate` method
Add `[Compare("StartDate")]`, which checks that one date follows another
Mark both properties `[DataType(DataType.Date)]` so the order is checked
