questions.why: `IValidatableObject.Validate` runs as part of model validation and can yield `ValidationResult`s naming the members involved. Attribute arguments must be constants, so `[Range]` cannot reference another property, and `[Compare]` checks equality, as for password confirmation.
questions.asked: Cross-field rules are the first thing attribute validation cannot express; knowing the hook is expected.

questions.q: What does the `errors` member look like in the 400 that ASP.NET Core returns for an invalid model?
choices: An array of strings, one message per failed rule, with no field names
A single string that joins every message with semicolons
An object keyed by field name, each holding an array of messages
An array of objects, each with `code`, `field` and `message` members
questions.why: `ValidationProblemDetails` extends RFC 9457 problem details with `errors`, a dictionary from member name to an array of messages, for example `{"Email": ["The Email field is required."]}`. Front ends map those keys back to form fields, which is why the shape matters.
questions.asked: Asked on fullstack roles because the React form code depends on this exact shape.

questions.q: FluentValidation's automatic ASP.NET Core integration is no longer recommended. What do its docs suggest instead?
choices: Registering validators as middleware so they run before routing
Converting every validator into DataAnnotations attributes
Running validators inside the JSON converter for each request type
Injecting `IValidator<T>` and calling `ValidateAsync` explicitly
questions.why: The auto-validation package hooked into MVC's synchronous validation pipeline, which cannot run async rules and does not exist for minimal APIs. Calling the validator explicitly, or from an endpoint or action filter, works everywhere and keeps async rules async.
questions.asked: FluentValidation is in most .NET codebases; knowing the current guidance shows you keep up.

questions.q: An update action binds the request directly to the `User` entity and saves it. What is the risk, and the fix?
choices: Only performance: binding an entity is slow, so switch to a record type
Overposting: a client can set `IsAdmin`; bind to a DTO and copy allowed fields
Concurrency: two updates clash, so wrap the save in a serializable transaction
Injection: bound strings reach SQL unescaped, so encode them before saving
questions.why: Binding to the entity lets any client set any mapped property, including roles or foreign keys, and `Update` marks every column modified. A request DTO with only editable fields closes the hole. EF Core parameterises values, so injection is not the issue here.
questions.asked: Overposting is a staple of .NET security questions and code reviews; the DTO is the expected answer.

questions.q: A .NET 9 Web API calls `builder.Services.AddOpenApi()` and `app.MapOpenApi()`. Where is the document served by default?
choices: At `/swagger/v1/swagger.json`, with Swagger UI at `/swagger`
At `/openapi/v1.json`, with no UI unless you add one yourself
At `/api-docs`, rendered as HTML by the built-in documentation page
Nowhere at runtime: the document is written to disk during build
questions.why: `Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi` serves the JSON document at `/openapi/{documentName}.json`, `v1` by default. The .NET 9 templates dropped Swashbuckle, so there is no UI; teams add Scalar or Swagger UI and point it at that URL. Build-time generation is a separate opt-in.
questions.asked: Checks you are current with .NET 9 templates rather than describing the Swashbuckle-era setup.

questions.q: A minimal API handler returns `IResult`. How do you make OpenAPI list its 200 and 404 responses without changing the return type?
choices: Add `.Produces<Order>(200)` and `.ProducesProblem(404)` to the endpoint
Put XML doc comments on the lambda so the generator reads the status codes
Throw exceptions for errors, since the generator documents thrown types
Add `[ApiController]` to Program.cs so the response types are inferred
questions.why: An `IResult` return carries no type information, so you add response metadata with `Produces`, `ProducesProblem` or `ProducesValidationProblem`. Returning `TypedResults` in a `Results<...>` union gives the same metadata automatically. The generator cannot see what a handler might throw.
questions.asked: Generated clients depend on accurate response metadata, so interviewers ask how you keep the document honest.

questions.q: What does `.WithName("GetOrder")` give a minimal API endpoint?
choices: A display name used only in the developer exception page
A route prefix, so the endpoint is served under `/GetOrder`
A name for link generation and the OpenAPI operationId
A policy name that authorization looks up for the endpoint
questions.why: Endpoint names must be unique and let `LinkGenerator` or `CreatedAtRoute` build URLs to the endpoint without hard-coding paths. The OpenAPI generator also uses the name as the `operationId`, which becomes the method name in generated clients.
questions.asked: Small detail, but generated-client method names come from it, which fullstack teams notice.

questions.q: You call `AddProblemDetails()`, yet `return TypedResults.NotFound();` still sends a 404 with an empty body. What adds a ProblemDetails body to it?
choices: `app.UseStatusCodePages()`, which fills in empty error bodies
`app.UseExceptionHandler()`, which catches every non-success status code
Nothing can: `NotFound()` always sends an empty body by design
`app.UseHttpLogging()`, which writes a body for responses that have none
questions.why: With `AddProblemDetails` registered, the status code pages middleware writes a ProblemDetails body for 4xx and 5xx responses that have no body. The exception handler deals only with exceptions. Alternatively return `TypedResults.Problem(...)` explicitly with the details you want.
questions.asked: Tests whether you know which middleware produces which error bodies, a common confusion.

questions.q: How do you add the current trace id to every ProblemDetails the app produces?
questions.code:
builder.Services.AddProblemDetails(o =>
    o.CustomizeProblemDetails = ctx => { /* ? */ });
choices: Throw a custom exception type that carries the trace id as a message
Add a JSON converter for `ProblemDetails` that writes an extra property
Set a `traceId` response header in middleware; bodies cannot be changed
Set `ctx.ProblemDetails.Extensions["traceId"]` in the callback
questions.why: `CustomizeProblemDetails` runs for every ProblemDetails written through `IProblemDetailsService`, and `Extensions` holds extra members that serialise at the top level. Including the trace id lets support match a user's error to the logs. A custom converter would be much more fragile.
questions.asked: Connects error responses to observability, which is what a mid-level answer should do.

questions.q: What route does this controller's `Get` action have?
choices: `api/OrdersController/{id}`, using the full class name as the token
`api/[controller]/{id}`, because tokens need `UseRouting` to be replaced
`api/Get/{id}`, because the action name replaces the controller token
`api/Orders/{id}`, since `[controller]` is the name minus the suffix
questions.why: Route tokens are replaced at startup: `[controller]` becomes the class name without the `Controller` suffix and `[action]` the method name. Matching is case-insensitive by default, so `/api/orders/5` works too.
questions.asked: Controllers basics; interviewers use it to check you can read attribute routing quickly.

questions.q: What does `CreatedAtAction(nameof(Get), new { id = order.Id }, order)` need to produce a correct `Location` header?
choices: An action called `Get` whose route accepts `id`, so a URL can be generated
A `[Location]` attribute on the `Order` class naming the property that holds its URL
An absolute base URL set in configuration under `Kestrel:Endpoints`
The `Get` action must be in a separate controller, or the name is ambiguous
questions.why: `CreatedAtAction` uses link generation to build the URL from the action name and route values; if no action matches, it throws when the result executes. There is no `[Location]` attribute, and link generation uses the current request's host.
questions.asked: Returning a proper 201 is a REST basic; the follow-up is usually 'what happens if the route values are wrong'.

questions.q: With default Kestrel limits, a client uploads a 50 MB file to an endpoint without size attributes. What happens?
choices: The upload succeeds, since Kestrel has no request body limit by default
It fails with 413 once the body passes the 30,000,000-byte limit
The request times out after 100 seconds and the client sees a 504
The body is truncated to 30 MB and the handler receives a partial file
questions.why: Kestrel's `MaxRequestBodySize` defaults to 30,000,000 bytes (about 28.6 MB); larger bodies are rejected with 413 Payload Too Large. Raise it per endpoint with `[RequestSizeLimit]` or `DisableRequestSizeLimit`, or globally in Kestrel options, and stream large files instead of buffering.
questions.asked: Upload features hit this in the first week; knowing the limit and the per-endpoint override is expected.

questions.q: What response does this minimal API endpoint send?
questions.code:
app.MapGet("/invoices/{id}/pdf", async (int id, InvoicePdf pdf) =>
    TypedResults.File(await pdf.RenderAsync(id), "application/pdf", $"invoice-{id}.pdf"));
choices: The PDF inline, with no filename, because a MIME type was supplied
A redirect to a temporary URL where the PDF can be downloaded
The bytes with `Content-Disposition: attachment` and that name
A JSON object whose `content` member holds the file as base64
questions.why: Passing a download name makes the file result set `Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=...`, so browsers save it. Omit the name to let the browser display it inline. File results write raw bytes, not JSON, and never redirect.
questions.asked: Downloads come up in every business app; interviewers check you know the header that controls them.

questions.q: What does a client receive from this .NET 8+ minimal API endpoint?
questions.code:
app.MapGet("/events", (EventStore store) => store.ReadAllAsync());
// ReadAllAsync returns IAsyncEnumerable<Event>
choices: Server-sent events, one `data:` line for each item as it is produced
A single JSON array streamed to the client as items are produced
Nothing until every item has been buffered into a list in memory
One HTTP response per item, sent over a kept-alive connection
questions.why: System.Text.Json serialises `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` as one JSON array and flushes as it goes, so the server does not buffer everything. It is still one ordinary JSON response, not an SSE stream; .NET 10 adds a separate `TypedResults.ServerSentEvents` result for that.
questions.asked: Large exports are a real requirement; streaming shows you think about memory on the server.

questions.q: Why can an ASP.NET Core controller return XML to one client and JSON to another, while a minimal API cannot out of the box?
choices: Controllers negotiate over registered formatters; minimal APIs write JSON
Minimal APIs ignore the `Accept` header only in Production builds for speed
Controllers serialise with Newtonsoft.Json, which can output XML natively
Minimal APIs negotiate too, but only between JSON and plain text formats
questions.why: MVC's output formatters pick a format from the `Accept` header (XML requires `AddXmlSerializerFormatters`). Minimal API results always write JSON for objects, which keeps them small and AOT-friendly. Controllers use System.Text.Json by default, not Newtonsoft.
questions.asked: A legitimate reason to keep controllers in some APIs; the interviewer wants trade-offs, not fashion.

questions.q: Why do minimal APIs work with Native AOT in .NET 8+ while MVC controllers do not?
choices: Controllers need the full framework, which AOT compilation cannot target
AOT supports only one route per app, and controllers register many
Minimal API binding can be source-generated; MVC relies on reflection
Minimal APIs run in the browser via WebAssembly, where AOT is required
questions.why: With AOT enabled, the Request Delegate Generator emits binding and response code at compile time, and JSON uses a source-generated `JsonSerializerContext`. MVC discovers controllers, filters and binders by reflection at runtime, which trimming breaks.
questions.asked: AOT is a common reason teams pick minimal APIs; knowing why shows you understand what the source generators do.

questions.q: What does `WebApplication.CreateSlimBuilder(args)` leave out compared with `CreateBuilder(args)`?
choices: Configuration from environment variables and command-line arguments
Dependency injection, so services must be constructed by hand
Kestrel, so the app must be hosted in IIS in-process instead
HTTPS, HTTP/3 and hosting-startup support, to stay small
questions.why: The slim builder is aimed at trimmed and AOT apps: it keeps DI, configuration, logging and Kestrel, but drops things like HTTPS and HTTP/3 support, `IHostingStartup` and some logging providers unless you add them back. Environment variables and command-line configuration still work.
questions.asked: Tests whether you know what the default builder does for you, which matters when a feature is missing in a slim app.

questions.q: In a container, which environment variable overrides `ConnectionStrings:Default` from appsettings.json?
choices: `ConnectionStrings:Default`, because colons are valid in variable names everywhere
`CONNECTIONSTRINGS_DEFAULT`, since keys are upper-cased and joined by one underscore
`ConnectionStrings__Default`, because a double underscore maps to the colon
`ConnectionStrings.Default`, because the provider maps dots to section separators
questions.why: The environment variables provider replaces `__` with `:` so nested keys work on every platform, including Linux shells that reject colons. Keys are case-insensitive, but a single underscore is kept as part of the name, and dots are not separators.
questions.asked: Everyone deploying to containers or Azure App Service needs this; getting it wrong means the app silently uses the dev value.

questions.q: `Limits:MaxItems` is 50 in appsettings.json, 100 in appsettings.Production.json, and the environment variable `Limits__MaxItems=200` is set. In Production with the default builder, what does the app read?
choices: 200, because environment variables are added after both JSON files
100, because the environment-specific file always has the final say
50, because appsettings.json is the base and is never overridden
An error at startup, because the same key is defined in three places
questions.why: Providers are layered and the last one added wins per key: appsettings.json, then appsettings.{Environment}.json, then user secrets in Development, then environment variables, then command-line arguments. Duplicate keys are the whole point of the layering, not an error.
questions.asked: Applied version of the provider-order question; interviewers use it to see if you can debug a wrong setting.

questions.q: Which statement about .NET user secrets is true?
choices: They are encrypted with the machine key and safe to use in production
They are stored in the repo under `secrets.json` but ignored by Git
They are loaded in every environment once `UserSecretsId` is present
They are plain JSON in your user profile, read only in Development
questions.why: `dotnet user-secrets` writes plain JSON under your user profile, outside the repo, and the default builder adds it only in Development. It keeps secrets out of Git on dev machines; production secrets come from the environment or a vault such as Azure Key Vault.
questions.asked: Checks you know user secrets are a dev convenience, not a production secret store.

questions.q: You set `ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT` to Staging in `Properties/launchSettings.json`. What does that change on the deployed server?
choices: The server runs as Staging, because the file is copied to the publish output
Nothing: launchSettings.json is only read by local tooling such as `dotnet run`
The server runs as Staging only when it is hosted in IIS rather than Kestrel
The value becomes the default whenever the server's own variable is missing
questions.why: launchSettings.json configures local launch profiles for `dotnet run`, Visual Studio and Rider; it is not published. On a server the environment comes from real environment variables, and when none is set the app runs as Production.
questions.asked: A common confusion when an app behaves differently on the server; the interviewer checks you know where the environment really comes from.

questions.q: With the default builder, what does `config.GetValue<int>("Limits:MaxItems")` return when the key does not exist?
choices: It throws `KeyNotFoundException` naming the missing key
It throws `InvalidOperationException` when the app starts
It returns 0, the default for `int`, without any error
It returns null, which makes the caller's `int` fail to compile
questions.why: `GetValue<T>` returns `default(T)` for a missing key, or the default you pass as its second argument. That is why silent zeros show up after a typo in a key name. Strongly typed options with validation make a missing value fail loudly instead.
questions.asked: Explains a whole category of 'the limit is somehow zero' bugs.

questions.q: appsettings.json has `"Origins": ["a.com", "b.com", "c.com"]` and appsettings.Production.json has `"Origins": ["prod.com"]`. What does `Origins` bind to in Production?
choices: `["prod.com"]`, because the later file replaces the whole array
`["a.com", "b.com", "c.com", "prod.com"]`, because arrays are concatenated
`["prod.com", "b.com", "c.com"]`, because array items merge by index
Nothing, because arrays in two files make the binder throw at startup
questions.why: Configuration flattens arrays into keys like `Origins:0`, `Origins:1`, and later providers override key by key. The production file only sets `Origins:0`, so indices 1 and 2 survive from the base file. Keep lists in one place, or use a delimited string you split yourself.
questions.asked: A real production incident pattern with CORS origins; knowing the flattening model is the deep answer.

questions.q: A singleton service takes `IOptionsSnapshot<SmtpOptions>` in its constructor. What happens in Development?
choices: The host throws, because a scoped service cannot be consumed from a singleton
It works and sees fresh values per request, because snapshots are thread-safe
It works but always sees the startup values, like `IOptions<T>` does
It compiles but throws `NullReferenceException` on the first `.Value` read
questions.why: `IOptionsSnapshot<T>` is registered as scoped, so scope validation in Development rejects it in a singleton. A singleton that needs current values should take `IOptionsMonitor<T>` and read `CurrentValue`, or subscribe with `OnChange`.
questions.asked: Combines the options interfaces with DI lifetimes, which is exactly how the bug appears in real code.

questions.q: Two blob containers are configured as named options. How does a service get the `images` settings?
questions.code:
builder.Services.Configure<BlobOptions>("images", config.GetSection("Blobs:Images"));
builder.Services.Configure<BlobOptions>("docs", config.GetSection("Blobs:Docs"));
choices: Inject `IOptions<BlobOptions>` and read `.Value`, which picks the first name
Inject `[FromKeyedServices("images")] BlobOptions`, since names become keys
Inject `IConfiguration` and bind `Blobs:Images` again, since names are lost
Inject `IOptionsMonitor<BlobOptions>` and call `.Get("images")`
questions.why: Named options are retrieved with `Get(name)` on `IOptionsMonitor<T>` or `IOptionsSnapshot<T>`. `IOptions<T>.Value` returns the default unnamed instance, which here was never configured. Options names are unrelated to keyed services.
questions.asked: Multi-tenant and multi-client configuration uses this; the interviewer checks you know the retrieval API.

questions.q: The config section is called `Smtp`, but a typo binds `Smpt`. What happens by default?
questions.code: builder.Services.AddOptions<SmtpOptions>().BindConfiguration("Smpt");
choices: The app fails at startup because the section `Smpt` cannot be found
The options bind with default property values and nothing reports it
The binder falls back to the closest section name and logs a warning
The first read of `.Value` throws `OptionsValidationException`
questions.why: Binding a missing section is not an error; you get an instance with default values, such as an empty host. Adding `ValidateDataAnnotations()` with `[Required]` members plus `ValidateOnStart()` turns the typo into a startup failure. Without validators nothing throws on `.Value` either.
questions.asked: Shows you would make misconfiguration fail fast instead of at 2 a.m. on the first email send.

questions.q: Why would a Native AOT app set `<EnableConfigurationBindingGenerator>` (on automatically with `PublishAot`)?
choices: It replaces JSON config files with compiled constants for faster startup
It lets configuration reload without restarting a trimmed application
It emits binding code at compile time, so no reflection is needed
It encrypts configuration values at build time so they are not readable
questions.why: The reflection-based binder breaks under trimming, so .NET 8 added a source generator that intercepts `Bind`, `Get` and `Configure` calls and generates the binding code. Configuration values are still read at runtime from the usual providers.
questions.asked: A niche but telling question for teams shipping AOT or trimmed services.

questions.q: You run the official .NET 8+ ASP.NET Core container image without setting any URLs. Which port does the app listen on?
choices: Port 80, the HTTP default, as the root user inside the container
Port 8080, since the images set `ASPNETCORE_HTTP_PORTS=8080`
Port 5000, the Kestrel default when nothing else is configured
Port 443 with a generated self-signed development certificate
questions.why: From .NET 8 the images default to port 8080 and include a non-root `app` user, since binding ports below 1024 needs root. Older images used 80, which is why upgraded deployments suddenly get connection refused until the port mapping or `ASPNETCORE_HTTP_PORTS` changes.
questions.asked: A real upgrade breakage; it shows hands-on container experience.

questions.q: Kubernetes sends SIGTERM to a .NET 9 API during a rolling deploy. What does the generic host do by default?
choices: It exits immediately, dropping in-flight requests; you must add a handler
It keeps serving new requests until the pod is killed with SIGKILL
It stops accepting connections and waits up to 30 s for work to finish
It waits for every hosted service to finish, however long that takes
questions.why: The host treats SIGTERM as a shutdown request: Kestrel stops taking new connections, in-flight requests drain and `StopAsync` runs on hosted services, bounded by `HostOptions.ShutdownTimeout`, which defaults to 30 seconds since .NET 8 (it was 5). Long background work must honour the stopping token.
questions.asked: Zero-downtime deploys depend on this; strong candidates mention the timeout and cancellation tokens.

questions.q: How does code outside a request react when the app begins shutting down?
choices: Catch `ThreadAbortException`, which the host raises in every thread
Poll `Environment.HasShutdownStarted` in a loop on a timer
Override `Finalize` on the service so it runs when the host stops
Use the `ApplicationStopping` token from `IHostApplicationLifetime`
questions.why: `IHostApplicationLifetime` exposes `ApplicationStarted`, `ApplicationStopping` and `ApplicationStopped` tokens. `BackgroundService` passes an equivalent token to `ExecuteAsync`. Thread aborts do not exist in modern .NET, and finalizers give no ordering guarantees.
questions.asked: Graceful shutdown is a production-readiness signal interviewers look for.

questions.q: An ASP.NET Core app runs on Windows behind IIS with the in-process hosting model. Which server handles the requests?
choices: IIS HTTP Server inside the IIS worker process; Kestrel is not used
Kestrel inside the IIS worker process, with IIS acting as a proxy
Kestrel in a separate process, with IIS forwarding over localhost
HTTP.sys directly, because IIS unloads when the app starts
questions.why: In-process hosting, the default for IIS, loads the app into `w3wp.exe` and uses the IIS HTTP Server (`IISHttpServer`). The out-of-process model is the one that runs Kestrel separately with IIS as a reverse proxy. HTTP.sys is a separate server option for Windows without IIS.
questions.asked: Still common in enterprise .NET shops; the answer shows you know hosting models, not just `dotnet run`.

questions.q: appsettings.json sets `"Logging:LogLevel:Microsoft.AspNetCore": "Warning"`. Which messages does that filter?
choices: Only logs from a class literally named `Microsoft.AspNetCore`
Every category starting with `Microsoft.AspNetCore`, below Warning
Every log in the app, since framework filters apply to all categories
Only HTTP request logs, since that category covers the Kestrel server
questions.why: Log filter keys match category prefixes, and the most specific match wins, so this silences Information and Debug logs from all ASP.NET Core categories while `Default` still governs your own. `ILogger<T>` uses the full type name as its category, which is why prefix rules work.
questions.asked: Tuning noisy framework logs is day-one production work.

questions.q: In a catch block, which call keeps the most useful information in structured logs?
choices: `logger.LogError(ex.Message)`
`logger.LogError($"Order {id} failed: {ex}")`
`logger.LogError(ex, "Order {OrderId} failed", id)`
`logger.LogError("Order {OrderId} failed: " + ex.StackTrace, id)`
questions.why: The overload that takes the exception first records it as a structured exception, with type, stack trace and inner exceptions, and `{OrderId}` becomes a searchable property. Interpolation or concatenation flattens everything into one string and loses the properties.
questions.asked: A basic that reveals whether you have ever searched production logs.

questions.q: What does `[LoggerMessage]` add over calling `logger.LogInformation("...", args)`?
choices: It sends the message to OpenTelemetry instead of the console provider
It encrypts the arguments so personal data never reaches the log sink
It makes the call asynchronous, so logging never blocks the request
Generated code that checks the level and avoids boxing and parsing
questions.why: The source generator parses the template at compile time and emits a strongly typed method that checks `IsEnabled` before doing any work, so there is no template parsing, `params` array or boxing per call. Providers and sinks are unchanged, and logging stays synchronous.
questions.asked: A performance-aware logging question; knowing the generator shows you have worked on hot paths.

questions.q: What does `logger.BeginScope` give you here, assuming a provider with scopes enabled?
choices: Each message carries an `OrderId` property without repeating it
The two messages are buffered and written as one entry when the block ends
Messages inside the block skip the level filter so they are always written
The block runs in its own thread so the logging does not slow the request
questions.why: A scope attaches its state to every log written while it is active, including logs from code you call. Providers must support scopes (for the console, `IncludeScopes`; OpenTelemetry has its own option). Scopes do not buffer, bypass filters or change threads.
questions.asked: Correlation is the core of useful logging; scopes are the .NET mechanism for it.

questions.q: What is the main risk of turning on `AddHttpLogging` with request and response bodies in production?
choices: It turns off response compression, which doubles bandwidth costs
It stops the exception handler from running for failed requests
It logs passwords, tokens and personal data, and costs throughput
It forces every response to HTTP/1.1, which breaks gRPC clients
questions.why: HTTP logging can write headers and bodies, which include credentials and personal data; it redacts unlisted headers by default but bodies are logged as-is. Buffering bodies also costs memory and latency. Log selected fields, and keep body logging for short debugging sessions.
questions.asked: Interviewers want to hear about PII in logs, which is a compliance problem, not only a performance one.

questions.q: You create spans with `new ActivitySource("Shop.Orders")`, but they never reach your OpenTelemetry backend while ASP.NET Core spans do. What is missing?
choices: Calling `Activity.Stop()` by hand, since `using` does not end spans
Registering the source with `.WithTracing(t => t.AddSource("Shop.Orders"))`
Setting `Activity.DefaultIdFormat` to W3C, which is off by default
Adding the source as a scoped service so each request gets its own
questions.why: The tracer provider only listens to sources it has been told about; with no listener, `StartActivity` returns null and nothing is recorded. Disposing the activity ends it, and W3C ids have been the default since .NET 5.
questions.asked: The most common reason custom tracing 'doesn't work'; knowing it shows real OpenTelemetry use.

questions.q: Why does this code use `?.` on the activity?
questions.code:
using var activity = Source.StartActivity("ReserveStock");
activity?.SetTag("order.id", orderId);
choices: `StartActivity` returns null when nothing listens, so tags need a guard
`SetTag` throws on a stopped activity, so the operator checks it is running
The operator is only for style; `StartActivity` never returns null
It avoids a race with the `using` statement disposing the activity early
questions.why: If no `ActivityListener` wants the source, or the sampler drops it, `StartActivity` returns null to avoid allocating. Unit tests usually have no listener, so unguarded calls throw there first. `SetTag` on a stopped activity is harmless.
questions.asked: Tests whether you have written instrumentation that runs in tests and production alike.

questions.q: For request duration in OpenTelemetry metrics, which instrument should you use?
choices: A `Counter<double>` that adds each duration, divided by the request count later
An `UpDownCounter<long>`, since durations can go up and down over time
An `ObservableGauge<double>` reporting the duration of the last request
A `Histogram<double>`, whose buckets give you percentiles
questions.why: Latency needs percentiles such as p95 and p99, which only a histogram's buckets provide; averages from a counter hide the slow tail. Gauges report a current value and would lose everything between scrapes. ASP.NET Core already emits `http.server.request.duration` as a histogram.
questions.asked: Distinguishes people who have built dashboards from people who have only read about metrics.

questions.q: Your API calls another service with an `HttpClient` from `IHttpClientFactory`, and both use OpenTelemetry. How does the downstream span join the same trace?
choices: The two services must share a table that stores the trace id
The client sends a `traceparent` header, which the server continues
Traces are matched afterwards by comparing timestamps in the backend
You must copy the trace id into a custom `X-Trace` header by hand
questions.why: HttpClient's diagnostics inject the W3C `traceparent` header from `Activity.Current`, and ASP.NET Core reads it to parent its request activity. No custom header or shared store is needed as long as both sides propagate W3C context.
questions.asked: Distributed tracing is expected knowledge for microservice roles; the header name is the concrete detail.

questions.q: What is the default `Timeout` of an `HttpClient` in .NET?
choices: 30 seconds, matching the host's default shutdown timeout
No timeout: requests wait until the server closes the socket
100 seconds, after which a `TaskCanceledException` is thrown
5 seconds, the recommended budget for calls inside a request
questions.why: `HttpClient.Timeout` defaults to 100 seconds, and a timeout surfaces as `TaskCanceledException` (with a `TimeoutException` inner exception since .NET 5). That is far too long inside a web request, so set a sensible timeout per client or use a resilience pipeline.
questions.asked: Slow dependencies take down APIs; interviewers check you know the default is dangerous.

questions.q: A typed client registered with `AddHttpClient<GeoClient>()` is injected into a singleton. What goes wrong over time?
choices: The singleton keeps one handler, so DNS changes are never seen
Each call creates a new socket, so the server runs out of ephemeral ports
The factory disposes the client after two minutes and later calls throw
Nothing: typed clients are designed to be captured by singletons
questions.why: Typed clients are transient; the factory rotates handlers (every two minutes by default) only for clients it creates. A singleton captures one client and its handler for good, missing DNS changes. Inject `IHttpClientFactory` into singletons, or use a static client with `SocketsHttpHandler.PooledConnectionLifetime`.
questions.asked: A follow-up to 'why IHttpClientFactory' that exposes whether you understand handler lifetime.

questions.q: What does `.AddStandardResilienceHandler()` from Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience add to an HttpClient?
choices: Automatic caching of GET responses according to `Cache-Control` headers
Retry, circuit breaker and total and per-attempt timeouts, with defaults
Client-side rate limiting that queues requests beyond a fixed quota
Request signing with a key stored in the Data Protection key ring
questions.why: The standard handler builds a Polly v8 pipeline: rate limiter, total timeout, retry with backoff, circuit breaker and per-attempt timeout, all configurable. It replaces hand-written Polly policies for most apps. It does not cache or sign requests.
questions.asked: Asked of anyone integrating third-party APIs; the modern answer is this package, not raw Polly.

questions.q: You add a retry pipeline to an HttpClient that creates payments with POST. What must you check first?
choices: That the client uses HTTP/2, since HTTP/1.1 cannot retry a request
That the retry count is odd, so a split vote never leaves the state unclear
That the server's clock matches, or the retried request is rejected as stale
That the endpoint is idempotent, for example via an idempotency key
questions.why: A timeout does not mean the server did nothing, so retrying a non-idempotent POST can charge twice. Either the API accepts an idempotency key or you exclude unsafe methods from retries (the resilience package offers `DisableForUnsafeHttpMethods()`).
questions.asked: Payments are the canonical example; interviewers want idempotency, not just 'add Polly'.

questions.q: What does `response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode()` do with a 404?
choices: It returns false, and you check the result before reading the body
It throws `HttpRequestException` with `StatusCode` set to 404
It retries the request once, then returns the second response
It logs a warning and lets you read the error body afterwards
questions.why: It throws for any non-2xx status, and since .NET 5 the exception's `StatusCode` property carries the code. If a 404 is an expected outcome, check `IsSuccessStatusCode` or the status yourself so you can read the ProblemDetails body instead of throwing.
questions.asked: Basic, but it leads into how you would surface a downstream error to your own caller.

questions.q: With default options, what does `MapHealthChecks("/health")` return when a check reports Degraded?
choices: 503 Service Unavailable, so the load balancer removes the instance
500 Internal Server Error with the failing check's exception
429 Too Many Requests, telling probes to back off for a while
200 OK with the text `Degraded` as the response body
questions.why: `HealthCheckOptions.ResultStatusCodes` maps Healthy and Degraded to 200 and Unhealthy to 503 by default. Degraded is meant for 'working but impaired', which should not pull the instance out of rotation. Change the mapping if your platform needs it.
questions.asked: Health endpoints drive orchestrator decisions; knowing the status mapping prevents accidental outages.

questions.q: In ASP.NET Core terms, what is the difference between authentication and authorisation?
choices: Authentication checks permissions; authorisation checks the password
Authentication says who the caller is; authorisation, what they may do
Authentication runs only for cookies; authorisation runs only for bearer tokens
Authentication happens in controllers; authorisation happens in middleware
questions.why: The authentication middleware turns a cookie or token into `HttpContext.User`; authorisation then evaluates policies against that user for the endpoint. Both apply to any scheme, and both run as middleware before the endpoint executes.
questions.asked: The most basic security vocabulary question; muddling the two is a red flag.

questions.q: When does ASP.NET Core answer 401 and when 403 for an `[Authorize(Roles = "Admin")]` endpoint?
choices: 401 for a signed-in non-admin; 403 when no credentials were sent
401 for an expired token; 403 for every other failure
401 when not authenticated; 403 when signed in but not an admin
403 in both cases, since the endpoint forbids everyone who is not an admin
questions.why: An anonymous caller gets a challenge (401 for bearer auth); an authenticated user who fails the policy gets forbid (403). Mixing them up confuses clients, which use 401 to trigger a sign-in and 403 to show 'no access'.
questions.asked: Clients depend on the difference; interviewers expect you to know which is which.

questions.q: A controller has `[Authorize]`, and one of its actions has `[AllowAnonymous]`. Who can call that action?
choices: Only authenticated users, because the controller attribute wins
Nobody, because the two attributes conflict and block the action
Only users with a role, because AllowAnonymous needs a role list
Anyone: AllowAnonymous skips authorisation for that action
questions.why: `[AllowAnonymous]` bypasses all authorisation checks for the endpoint, even when `[Authorize]` sits on the controller or a fallback policy exists. That makes it powerful and worth reviewing, because it also overrides stricter policies placed higher up.
questions.asked: A quick check on attribute precedence, which matters when auditing endpoints.

questions.q: What does `.RequireAuthorization()` with no arguments do to this minimal API endpoint?
questions.code: app.MapGet("/orders", GetOrders).RequireAuthorization();
choices: Applies the default policy, which requires an authenticated user
Requires the Admin role, the default role for protected endpoints
Requires an API key header, checked before authentication runs
Nothing until `[Authorize]` is also added to the handler method
questions.why: Without a policy name, `RequireAuthorization()` adds the default policy, which out of the box just requires an authenticated user. Pass a policy name for anything stricter. It is the minimal API equivalent of `[Authorize]`.
questions.asked: Everyday minimal API security; the follow-up is usually about named policies.

questions.q: Who can call an action marked `[Authorize(Roles = "Admin,Manager")]`?
choices: Only users who hold both the Admin and the Manager role
Users in either the Admin or the Manager role
Users whose single role claim is exactly "Admin,Manager"
Anyone authenticated, because Roles is only documentation
questions.why: A comma-separated list inside one attribute means any of the roles. To require both, stack two attributes, `[Authorize(Roles = "Admin")]` and `[Authorize(Roles = "Manager")]`, because separate attributes must all pass.
questions.asked: A small syntax point with security consequences if misread.

questions.q: A React app and its ASP.NET Core API share a site. Why do many teams prefer an HttpOnly auth cookie over storing a JWT in localStorage?
choices: Cookies are encrypted by the browser, while localStorage is sent as plain text
Cookies never need CSRF protection, unlike tokens kept in localStorage
JWTs cannot be used by React apps because browsers block the Authorization header
Script cannot read an HttpOnly cookie, so an XSS bug cannot steal the session
questions.why: Anything in localStorage is readable by any script on the page, so one XSS flaw leaks the token. An HttpOnly cookie is sent automatically but hidden from JavaScript. The trade-off is that cookie auth needs SameSite and antiforgery defences against CSRF.
questions.asked: A standard SPA security question; strong answers mention the CSRF trade-off too.

questions.q: In a controller action, how do you read the signed-in user's id when it is issued as the name identifier claim?
choices: `User.Identity.Name`, which always holds the user's id
`HttpContext.Session["UserId"]`, set by the authentication middleware
`User.FindFirstValue(ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier)`
`Request.Headers["UserId"]`, added to each authenticated request
questions.why: `User` is the `ClaimsPrincipal` built by authentication, and `FindFirstValue` reads a claim. `Identity.Name` comes from the name claim, which is often an email or display name. Never trust a user id sent in a header or body.
questions.asked: Getting the current user safely is in almost every endpoint that touches owned data.

questions.q: Your API has no CORS policy, yet calls from Postman and from another server succeed. Why?
choices: CORS is enforced by browsers; other clients ignore it
ASP.NET Core allows every origin until a policy is configured
Postman and servers send a secret header that bypasses CORS
CORS applies only to POST requests, and those calls were GETs
questions.why: CORS is a browser mechanism that decides whether page script may read a cross-origin response. Non-browser clients are unaffected, so CORS is not access control; authentication and authorisation are. Without a policy, browsers block cross-origin reads.
questions.asked: Clears up the most common CORS misconception: that it protects the API.

questions.q: A React app on another origin sends `fetch(url, { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, body })`. What does the browser do first?
choices: Sends the POST directly, because JSON is a simple content type
Sends an OPTIONS preflight to ask if the method and headers are allowed
Sends a HEAD request to check the endpoint exists before the POST
Blocks the request outright, because cross-origin POSTs are never allowed
questions.why: `application/json` is not one of the CORS-safelisted content types, so the browser preflights with OPTIONS and only sends the POST if the response allows the origin, method and headers. The CORS middleware answers preflights for you when the policy matches.
questions.asked: Explains the mysterious OPTIONS requests in the network tab, and what must be allowed.

questions.q: What does `app.UseHttpsRedirection()` do, and why is it not enough on its own for an API?
choices: It encrypts HTTP traffic in place; APIs also need a certificate on the client
It turns HTTP into HTTPS inside Kestrel, so no redirect ever reaches clients
It forces TLS 1.3, which some API clients do not yet support
It redirects to HTTPS, but API clients may already have sent secrets
questions.why: The middleware answers HTTP requests with a redirect to HTTPS. Browsers follow it, but an API client has already sent its token or body in clear text, and many clients do not follow redirects for POST. For APIs, do not listen on HTTP, or reject it.
questions.asked: Shows you think about what actually travels over the wire, not just the green padlock.

questions.q: What does this fallback policy change?
choices: Endpoints with no auth metadata require a signed-in user
Endpoints with `[Authorize]` now also require the Admin role
Anonymous users are redirected to a fallback login page
Failed policies fall back to allowing the request after logging
questions.why: The fallback policy applies to endpoints with neither `[Authorize]` nor `[AllowAnonymous]`, making the app secure by default: a new endpoint someone forgets to protect is still locked. Public endpoints then opt out explicitly.
questions.asked: Secure-by-default configuration is a mature habit interviewers look for.

questions.q: Two authorisation handlers are registered for the same requirement. One calls `context.Succeed(requirement)`; the other does nothing. What is the outcome?
choices: Denied, because every handler must call Succeed for the requirement
Denied, because a handler that does nothing counts as a failure
Allowed, because one handler succeeding satisfies the requirement
It depends on registration order, as the last handler decides
questions.why: Handlers for one requirement act as alternatives: any `Succeed` satisfies it, and doing nothing is neutral. Only an explicit `context.Fail()` vetoes it regardless of others. Separate requirements in a policy must all be satisfied.
questions.asked: Explains how to model 'owner or admin' rules with multiple handlers.

questions.q: An action has both `[Authorize(Policy = "Employee")]` and `[Authorize(Policy = "FinanceTeam")]`. What must the user satisfy?
choices: Either policy; ASP.NET Core picks whichever passes first
Only the policy declared last, which overrides the earlier one
Only the policy declared first, as the others are ignored
Each of the two, since every `[Authorize]` attribute must pass
questions.why: Multiple `[Authorize]` attributes (on the action, controller or endpoint) combine with AND: all of them must succeed. For OR logic, write one policy whose requirement has several handlers, or use `RequireAssertion`.
questions.asked: Combining attributes is common; getting AND versus OR wrong opens or closes the wrong doors.

questions.q: A JWT's `exp` time passed three minutes ago. With default `TokenValidationParameters`, does `AddJwtBearer` accept it?
choices: No: expired tokens are rejected from the first second
Yes: the default clock skew allows five minutes after expiry
Yes: expiry is not checked unless `ValidateLifetime` is set
No: the token is rejected and the refresh endpoint is called
questions.why: `ClockSkew` defaults to five minutes to tolerate clock drift between issuer and API, so tokens live a little longer than `exp` says. Lower it (for example to 30 seconds) when short-lived tokens matter. `ValidateLifetime` is on by default.
questions.asked: A classic 'why does my expired token still work?' question in real projects.

questions.q: A token carries a `sub` claim, but `User.FindFirst("sub")` returns null with default JwtBearer settings. Why?
choices: It is mapped to `ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier`; `MapInboundClaims = false` keeps it
The `sub` claim is stripped for privacy, so it never reaches the ClaimsPrincipal
Claims are only populated after `UseAuthorization`, which runs after the endpoint
`FindFirst` is case-sensitive, and the handler stores the claim as `SUB`
questions.why: By default the JWT handler maps short claim names to the long legacy `ClaimTypes` URIs, so `sub` becomes `.../nameidentifier`. Read that type, or disable the mapping with `MapInboundClaims = false` to keep the token's names.
questions.asked: A confusing default that nearly everyone hits; knowing it saves hours.

questions.q: Every JSON call from the SPA on another origin is preceded by an OPTIONS request, adding a round trip each time. Which CORS policy setting reduces that?
choices: `AllowAnyMethod()`, which tells browsers to stop sending preflights
`SetPreflightMaxAge(...)`, so browsers cache the preflight answer
`WithExposedHeaders("*")`, which merges the preflight into the call
`DisallowCredentials()`, as preflights are only sent with cookies
questions.why: The policy's preflight max age becomes `Access-Control-Max-Age`, letting the browser reuse a successful preflight for that URL for a while (browsers cap the value). Allowing methods or exposing headers changes what is permitted, not whether a preflight is needed.
questions.asked: Shows you can tune CORS for latency once it works, not just make the error go away.

questions.q: Only `/api/public` should be callable cross-origin. How do you apply a named CORS policy to just that group of minimal API endpoints?
choices: Call `app.UseCors("Spa")` a second time after mapping the group
Add `.RequireCors("Spa")` to the group and keep `app.UseCors()`
Add an `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` header in each handler
Name the route group "Spa" so it matches the policy by convention
questions.why: Endpoint-level CORS uses `RequireCors(policyName)` (or `[EnableCors]` on controllers), and the CORS middleware without a default policy applies it per endpoint. Setting headers by hand skips preflight handling and is easy to get wrong.
questions.asked: Scoping CORS narrowly is better security than opening the whole app.

questions.q: An app runs on three instances behind a load balancer. Users are randomly signed out and antiforgery checks fail. What is the likely cause?
choices: Each instance has its own Data Protection keys and cannot read others' cookies
The load balancer strips cookies larger than 4 KB from every forwarded request
Session state is stored per instance, so authentication is lost when it moves
Kestrel limits the number of cookies per request when behind a proxy
questions.why: Auth cookies and antiforgery tokens are encrypted with Data Protection keys, which by default live on each machine. Persist keys to shared storage (for example `PersistKeysToDbContext` or blob storage) and set one application name so every instance can decrypt them.
questions.asked: A classic scale-out bug; the fix shows you understand what protects cookies.

questions.q: Why does a cookie-authenticated form endpoint need antiforgery protection when a bearer-token API usually does not?
choices: Bearer tokens are encrypted by TLS, while cookies travel in plain text
Cookie endpoints accept form posts, which browsers cannot send securely
Antiforgery also validates the token signature, which cookies lack
Browsers attach cookies to cross-site requests; tokens need your script
questions.why: CSRF works because the browser sends cookies with requests that another site triggers. A bearer token must be attached by your own script, which the attacker's page cannot do. SameSite cookies reduce the risk, and antiforgery tokens close it.
questions.asked: Tests whether you understand CSRF as a property of cookies, not of forms.

questions.q: What does this rate-limiting partition achieve?
choices: One shared limit of 100 per minute for the whole application
A limit of 100 per minute per endpoint, whoever calls it
100 a minute for each user, or per IP for anonymous callers
100 requests in total per user, reset only when the app restarts
questions.why: The partition key picks which limiter a request uses, so each user name (or IP) gets its own fixed window. Without partitioning, one noisy client could exhaust a global limit for everyone. Behind a proxy, configure forwarded headers so the IP is the client's.
questions.asked: Per-client limits are the realistic design; interviewers look for the partition idea.

questions.q: A fixed window allows 100 requests per minute. Why might a team switch to a sliding window or token bucket limiter?
choices: Fixed windows allow a burst of 200 around a window boundary
Fixed windows cannot be partitioned by user or IP address
Fixed windows reject requests with 500 instead of 429
Fixed windows keep one timer per request, using lots of memory
questions.why: A client can send 100 at the end of one window and 100 at the start of the next. Sliding windows split the period into segments, and token buckets refill steadily, both smoothing bursts. Every limiter type can be partitioned, and the rejection code is configurable.
questions.asked: Shows you understand algorithm behaviour, not just the configuration API.

questions.q: Rate-limiting policies attached with `RequireRateLimiting("per-user")` are ignored. The pipeline calls `app.UseRateLimiter()` before `app.UseRouting()`. Why?
choices: Named policies apply only to controllers, never to minimal APIs
Before routing, no endpoint is chosen, so its metadata is unseen
The limiter needs `UseAuthorization` to run first to read the user
Policies take effect only after the first minute of uptime
questions.why: Endpoint-specific policies are metadata on the selected endpoint, which exists only after routing. With an explicit `UseRouting`, put `UseRateLimiter` after it. Global limiters do not depend on the endpoint and work anywhere.
questions.asked: Middleware order bugs are subtle; this checks you reason from endpoint metadata.

questions.q: `AddJwtBearer` is configured with `Authority = "https://login.example.com/"` and no signing key. How does it validate signatures?
choices: It does not: tokens are trusted whenever the issuer claim matches
It sends each token back to the authority to check it on every request
It uses the TLS certificate of the authority as the signing key
It fetches the issuer's published signing keys and refreshes them
questions.why: With an `Authority`, the handler reads `.well-known/openid-configuration`, fetches the JWKS signing keys, caches them and refreshes periodically, so key rotation just works. Validation is local; there is no per-request call to the issuer.
questions.asked: Explains how APIs trust an identity provider without sharing secrets.

questions.q: An `IClaimsTransformation` adds a `permission` claim from the database. Why must it be written to be idempotent?
choices: It can run more than once per request, so it must not duplicate claims
It runs once at start-up, so the claims it adds must never change afterwards
It runs before authentication, so the user may still be anonymous
It runs on a background thread, so it must avoid scoped services
questions.why: `TransformAsync` runs each time authentication is evaluated, which can happen more than once per request, so blindly adding claims duplicates them. Check before adding, or clone the principal. It also runs per request, so cache database lookups.
questions.asked: A deeper hook that interviewers use to see whether you read how it is invoked.

questions.q: In .NET 10, a signed-out client calls a cookie-authenticated minimal API endpoint that returns JSON. What does it get by default?
choices: A 302 redirect to `/Account/Login`, exactly as in earlier versions
A 200 with an empty body, because the endpoint allows anonymous reads
A 401, as cookie auth no longer redirects for known API endpoints
A 404, so the endpoint's existence is hidden from anonymous callers
questions.why: Earlier versions redirected any unauthenticated cookie request to the login page, which API clients read as a confusing 200 or 302. .NET 10 returns 401/403 for endpoints recognised as APIs, such as minimal APIs returning data and `[ApiController]` actions; pages still redirect.
questions.asked: Shows you follow recent framework changes that affect SPA and API behaviour.

questions.q: What does this cache call do on the first and on later requests within five minutes?
choices: Calls the API every time and stores the latest result for other callers
Calls the API once, then serves the cached value for five minutes
Calls the API once and keeps the value until the app restarts
Serves the cached value and refreshes it in the background every time
questions.why: `GetOrCreateAsync` runs the factory only on a miss and stores the result with the entry's options. Absolute expiration removes it five minutes after creation, and the next call fetches again. `IMemoryCache` never refreshes entries in the background by itself.
questions.asked: Cache-aside with expiry is the most common caching pattern in CRUD apps.

questions.q: In .NET 8+, what is needed for `.CacheOutput()` on this endpoint to take effect?
questions.code: app.MapGet("/products", GetProducts).CacheOutput();
choices: `builder.Services.AddOutputCache()` and `app.UseOutputCache()`
A `Cache-Control: public` header added by the handler itself
`builder.Services.AddMemoryCache()` so responses have somewhere to go
Nothing else; the attribute alone stores the response on the client
questions.why: Output caching needs its services and middleware; the endpoint call only adds metadata. The server then stores whole responses (60 seconds by default) and replays them without running the handler. It does not depend on client headers.
questions.asked: Checks you know output caching is a server-side feature with its own middleware.

questions.q: What does `IDistributedCache` store, and why use a Redis-backed one?
choices: Strongly typed objects; Redis keeps them in the app's own memory
Only strings; Redis is required because SQL Server cannot store bytes
Byte arrays by key; a shared store keeps every instance consistent
Whole HTTP responses; Redis replays them to clients automatically
questions.why: `IDistributedCache` is a key/byte[] abstraction (with string helpers), so you serialise values yourself. Backing it with Redis (`AddStackExchangeRedisCache`) or SQL Server gives all instances one cache that survives restarts.
questions.asked: Leads into the in-memory versus distributed trade-off every scaled app faces.

questions.q: Products are cached for ten minutes under `product:{id}`. After an admin edits a product, what should the update endpoint do?
choices: Nothing; the stale entry is harmless until it expires
Clear the entire cache so no entry can be stale
Restart the app so the cache is rebuilt from scratch
Remove that product's cache entry after saving
questions.why: Invalidate the specific key once the write commits, so the next read loads fresh data. Wiping everything causes a load spike, and waiting for expiry shows admins their old values. On multiple instances, local caches each need invalidating, which is where distributed caches help.
questions.asked: Cache invalidation is famously hard; interviewers want to see a concrete strategy.

questions.q: Which is the idiomatic way to run work every five minutes inside a `BackgroundService` in .NET 6+?
choices: `while (true) { Thread.Sleep(300_000); DoWork(); }` on the host thread
A `System.Timers.Timer` whose callback is an async void method
A `PeriodicTimer` loop: `while (await timer.WaitForNextTickAsync(ct))`
Recursion: ExecuteAsync calls itself after a `Task.Delay` of five minutes
questions.why: `PeriodicTimer` gives an async, cancellable tick loop that never overlaps runs and stops cleanly on shutdown. `Thread.Sleep` blocks a thread and ignores cancellation, async void timer callbacks swallow exceptions and can overlap, and recursion grows state.
questions.asked: A small but modern API choice that shows you write clean hosted services.

questions.q: A cached dashboard query is keyed as `"dashboard"`, but its data depends on the signed-in user's tenant. What goes wrong?
choices: The cache throws, because keys must include a user id
Every tenant is served whichever tenant's data was cached first
Nothing, since memory caches are separate for each user session
The entry expires at once, because tenant claims change each request
questions.why: A cache is shared across requests, so a key must include everything the value depends on, such as tenant id, user id or culture. Otherwise one customer sees another's data, which is a security incident rather than a performance bug.
questions.asked: Checks that you treat cache keys as a data-isolation concern.

questions.q: An endpoint starts `_ = Task.Run(() => SendReceiptAsync(db, order));` and returns at once. The task later fails with `ObjectDisposedException`. Why?
choices: The DbContext belongs to the request scope, disposed when it ends
Task.Run tasks are cancelled automatically when the HTTP response is sent
SendReceiptAsync must be marked static to run on a background thread
The thread pool disposes objects that are captured by lambda closures
questions.why: Scoped services live until the request finishes, but the fire-and-forget task outlives it. Hand the work to a queue processed by a hosted service that creates its own scope. Failures in unobserved tasks are also silently lost.
questions.asked: Fire-and-forget in controllers is a common bug; this checks you know why and what to do instead.

questions.q: How does output caching differ from caching data with `IMemoryCache` inside the handler?
choices: Output caching stores the whole HTTP response and skips the handler
Output caching stores data in the browser; IMemoryCache on the server
Output caching only works for POST; IMemoryCache only for GET
Output caching needs Redis, while IMemoryCache never needs any setup
questions.why: Output caching replays serialised responses without running the endpoint, which is ideal for identical public responses. `IMemoryCache` caches objects your code chooses, so it can serve personalised responses built from shared data. Output caching can use memory or Redis.
questions.asked: Picking the right caching layer is a design decision interviewers like to probe.

questions.q: Why should a `BackgroundService` loop pass `stoppingToken` to `Task.Delay` and to its I/O calls?
choices: Without it, the delay runs on the UI thread and freezes the app
The token makes the delay more accurate on busy servers
So shutdown cancels the waits and the host can stop promptly
The token is required, or the service never starts at all
questions.why: `stoppingToken` is cancelled when the host begins shutting down. Passing it through lets waits and queries end quickly instead of holding up shutdown until the host's timeout, after which work is abandoned mid-way.
questions.asked: Graceful shutdown matters in containers; this checks the basic habit.

questions.q: What does `HybridCache` (.NET 9) combine behind one `GetOrCreateAsync` API?
choices: Output caching and response caching for HTTP responses
A local in-memory cache with an optional distributed cache
Browser storage and a server cache, synchronised over SignalR
EF Core's second-level cache and the change tracker
questions.why: `HybridCache` keeps a fast in-process layer and, when an `IDistributedCache` is registered, a shared second layer. It also handles serialisation and stops concurrent callers from running the same factory at once.
questions.asked: A newer API that replaces a lot of hand-written cache-aside code.

questions.q: By default, which of these responses does output caching store?
choices: Every GET, including those with an Authorization header
A POST that returns 201 Created with the new resource
A 200 GET for an anonymous request with no cookies
A GET that returns 200 and sets a Set-Cookie header
questions.why: The default policy caches only GET/HEAD requests answered with 200, and skips authenticated requests and responses that set cookies, to avoid serving one user's data to another. Custom policies can change this, carefully.
questions.asked: Knowing the safe defaults explains why caching 'does nothing' on authenticated endpoints.

questions.q: Endpoints need to enqueue emails for a `BackgroundService` to send. What is a good in-process building block for the queue?
choices: A static `List<Email>` that the service polls every second
A singleton `Channel<Email>` that endpoints write to
A scoped `Queue<Email>` injected into both endpoints and service
`ConcurrentBag<Email>`, drained whenever the service is idle
questions.why: `Channel<T>` is a thread-safe async producer/consumer queue: endpoints `WriteAsync`, the service `await foreach` over `ReadAllAsync`, with no polling. A bounded channel adds back-pressure. A scoped queue would be a different instance per request.
questions.asked: Shows you can build a simple, correct in-process queue without extra infrastructure.

questions.q: Since .NET 6, what happens by default when a `BackgroundService` throws an unhandled exception from `ExecuteAsync`?
choices: The exception is logged and the host stops the application
The exception is swallowed and the service restarts silently
The service stops quietly while the rest of the app keeps running
The exception is rethrown inside the next HTTP request
questions.why: `BackgroundServiceExceptionBehavior.StopHost` is the default, so a crashing worker takes the app down and gets noticed. Before .NET 6 the service died silently. Catch and log per iteration if the loop should survive transient errors.
questions.asked: A behaviour change many teams discover in production; knowing it prevents surprises.

questions.q: Emails are queued in an in-memory `Channel<T>`. What is the main risk, and when do teams move beyond it?
choices: Channels drop items after one minute, so slow consumers lose work
Channels block every request until the email has been sent
Channels only work in Development, as production hosts disable them
Queued work is lost on restart or crash; durable queues fix that
questions.why: An in-memory queue disappears with the process, including during every deployment. When losing a job matters, persist it: a database table (outbox), Hangfire, or a broker such as Azure Service Bus or RabbitMQ, which also spread work across instances.
questions.asked: Tests whether you match the tool to the durability the business needs.

questions.q: Two hundred requests miss the cache for the same key at once. What does `HybridCache.GetOrCreateAsync` do that a naive `IMemoryCache` check-then-set does not?
choices: It runs the factory once; the other callers await that result
It rejects the extra callers with 429 until the entry is stored
It runs all 200 factories and keeps the result of the fastest
It serves null to the extra callers until the entry is ready
questions.why: HybridCache coalesces concurrent requests for the same key, preventing a cache stampede where every caller hits the database together. With plain `IMemoryCache.GetOrCreateAsync`, concurrent misses can each run the factory.
questions.asked: Stampede protection separates caching that helps under load from caching that collapses.

questions.q: Product list responses are output-cached with a tag. How do you evict them when a product changes?
questions.code:
app.MapGet("/products", GetProducts)
   .CacheOutput(p => p.Tag("products"));
choices: Call `IMemoryCache.Remove("products")` in the update endpoint
Call `EvictByTagAsync("products", ct)` on `IOutputCacheStore`
Send `Cache-Control: no-cache` from the update endpoint's response
Restart the output cache middleware with `app.UseOutputCache()`
questions.why: Tags group cached responses so a write can evict all of them through `IOutputCacheStore`. Output cache entries are not in `IMemoryCache` under your key, and response headers on another endpoint do not affect them.
questions.asked: Invalidation is the hard part of output caching; tags are the intended tool.

questions.q: `/products?page=2` and `/products?page=3` should be cached separately, but `?utm_source=...` should not create new entries. What fits?
choices: `.CacheOutput(p => p.VaryByQuery("page"))`
`.CacheOutput(p => p.NoCache())` on the product list
`.CacheOutput(p => p.VaryByHeader("page"))`
`.CacheOutput(p => p.Expire(TimeSpan.Zero))` per page
questions.why: `VaryByQuery` names the query keys that form part of the cache key, so only `page` creates separate entries. `VaryByHeader` looks at request headers, not the query, and `NoCache` or zero expiry turn caching off.
questions.asked: Cache key design decides hit rate; this checks you can tune it.

questions.q: An endpoint uses `.WithRequestTimeout(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2))` with `app.UseRequestTimeouts()` (.NET 8+). How does the timeout take effect?
choices: The handler's thread is aborted after two seconds
Kestrel closes the TCP connection after two seconds
`RequestAborted` is cancelled; code must observe it for the 504
The request is retried once on another thread after two seconds
questions.why: The middleware cancels `HttpContext.RequestAborted`; handlers that pass that token (or a bound `CancellationToken`) to their I/O stop, and the middleware then writes a 504 by default. Code that ignores the token keeps running. .NET never aborts threads.
questions.asked: Shows you understand cooperative cancellation in .NET, which timeouts rely on.

questions.q: A nightly clean-up runs as a `BackgroundService`. After scaling to three instances, it runs three times a night. What are sensible fixes?
choices: Add `[Singleton]` to the class so only one instance ever runs it
Register the service as scoped so each request gets its own run
Increase the timer interval to 24 hours on two of the instances
Use a distributed lock, or one scheduler outside the web app
questions.why: Every instance runs every hosted service. Coordinate with a lease or lock in the database or Redis, use a job library such as Hangfire or Quartz with clustering, or move the job to a single scheduled worker. DI lifetimes do not span processes.
questions.asked: Scaling out breaks singleton assumptions; interviewers want to see you anticipate that.

questions.q: Why is sliding expiration alone risky for a popular cache entry?
choices: Sliding expiration removes an entry on every read, so it never hits
Each read extends the entry, so hot data may never refresh
Sliding expiration is ignored unless a size limit is also configured
Sliding entries are evicted first whenever the process needs memory
questions.why: Sliding expiration resets on each access, so a value read every minute lives forever and goes stale. Combine it with an absolute expiration that caps the lifetime, or rely on absolute expiry for data that changes.
questions.asked: A subtle staleness bug; the fix shows you understand both expiry modes.

questions.q: In .NET 8 and 9, a `BackgroundService` does 20 seconds of synchronous work before its first `await`. What happens at start-up?
choices: Nothing unusual, because hosted services always start on the thread pool
The app starts, and the service is skipped until the work completes
The host throws, because ExecuteAsync must await within a second
Start-up waits: the synchronous part runs inside StartAsync
questions.why: In those versions `StartAsync` calls `ExecuteAsync` directly, so everything before the first real await runs on the start-up path and delays the host (.NET 10 runs ExecuteAsync as a background task instead). Start with `await Task.Yield()` or move heavy work after an await.
questions.asked: A subtle start-up delay that shows you know how hosted services are invoked.

questions.q: `HybridCache` entries for products are stored with the tag `"catalogue"`. What does `await cache.RemoveByTagAsync("catalogue")` do?
choices: Removes only entries whose key string contains the word catalogue
Invalidates every entry with that tag, so the next reads refetch
Clears the distributed layer but leaves stale entries in memory
Blocks new writes to the catalogue until the app restarts
questions.why: Tags let you invalidate a group of entries without knowing their keys, and HybridCache honours the invalidation in both layers for later reads. Keys are not searched by text, and nothing is blocked.
questions.asked: Group invalidation is what makes caching maintainable as features grow.

questions.q: Why is response compression over HTTPS disabled by default in ASP.NET Core (`EnableForHttps = false`)?
choices: TLS already compresses the payload, so a second pass is wasted work
Browsers cannot decompress a Brotli response sent over HTTPS
Compressing secrets beside attacker input can leak them
Compression breaks HTTP/2 multiplexing when TLS is in use
questions.why: Attacks such as CRIME and BREACH infer secrets from compressed sizes when a response mixes secrets and attacker-controlled data. Enable it for HTTPS only when responses do not do that, or rely on a proxy or CDN. TLS itself no longer compresses.
questions.asked: Tests whether you know that a performance switch can have security costs.

questions.q: After setting `SizeLimit = 1000` on the memory cache options, a call to `cache.Set(key, value)` without options throws. Why?
choices: With a size limit, every entry must declare its own Size
Set requires an expiration whenever a size limit exists
The limit is measured in megabytes, and the value is too large
Keys must be integers once a size limit has been configured
questions.why: `SizeLimit` has no units; the cache just sums the `Size` you assign to each entry, so an entry without a size cannot be accounted for and is rejected. Choose a unit (items, approximate bytes) and set it everywhere, or do not use a limit.
questions.asked: A surprising runtime error that shows whether you have bounded a cache in practice.

questions.q: With default options, which files does `app.UseStaticFiles()` serve?
choices: Any file in the project folder, including appsettings.json
Files under the web root, wwwroot by default, by their path
Only the files listed in a manifest generated at build time
Files anywhere on disk, if the request path is an absolute one
questions.why: The static files middleware maps request paths onto the web root (wwwroot unless configured), so `/css/site.css` serves `wwwroot/css/site.css`. Files outside it, such as appsettings.json, are not exposed, which is why the web root must hold only public assets.
questions.asked: A basic hosting question that doubles as a security check on what the app exposes.

questions.q: A middleware resolves the tenant for each request, and the endpoint needs it. What is `HttpContext.Items` for in this situation?
choices: A cache shared by all requests, cleared when the app restarts
A per-request dictionary for passing data along the pipeline
A list of the middleware registered for the current endpoint
A cookie store that persists values between separate requests
questions.why: `Items` lives exactly as long as one request, so middleware can stash a value that later middleware or the endpoint reads. It is not shared between requests and is never sent to the client. A scoped service holding the tenant is a typed alternative.
questions.asked: Checks you know the right place for request-scoped data between middleware and endpoints.

questions.q: Which is a common, explicit way to version a public REST API built with ASP.NET Core?
choices: Change the response shape silently and let clients adapt
Create a separate database for each version of the API
Put it in the URL, such as `/v2/orders`, or in a header
Rename every endpoint on each release so old names stop working
questions.why: URL segments, a query parameter or a header all make the version explicit, and the Asp.Versioning packages support each for controllers and minimal APIs. Versioning lets old clients keep working while new ones adopt breaking changes.
questions.asked: Opens a discussion about breaking changes and how you support existing clients.

questions.q: A list endpoint takes `pageSize` from the query string. Why should it cap the value?
questions.code: app.MapGet("/orders", (int page = 1, int pageSize = 20) => ...);
choices: Kestrel rejects query values larger than 100 with a 400 anyway
EF Core cannot translate `Take` for values above 1,000
Paging only works when pageSize is a power of two
A client could ask for a million rows and exhaust the server
questions.why: Unbounded page sizes let one request load huge result sets into memory and hold database resources. Clamp to a sensible maximum (for example 100) and document it. Kestrel and EF impose no such limit for you.
questions.asked: A small defensive habit that shows you think about abuse, not just the happy path.

questions.q: What should a successful minimal API DELETE endpoint usually return when there is nothing to send back?
choices: `TypedResults.NoContent()`, a 204 with an empty body
`TypedResults.Ok()`, a 200 whose body is `null` JSON
`TypedResults.Accepted()`, since deletes complete later
`TypedResults.Created()`, since the state has changed
questions.why: 204 No Content says the action succeeded and there is no body. 202 means the work has not finished, which is untrue here, and 201 is for new resources. Returning 404 when the row count is 0 is a common refinement.
questions.asked: Status code choices are part of API design interviews; 204 for deletes is the expected default.

questions.q: Why does this controller action fail at start-up or on the first request?
questions.code:
[HttpPost]
public IActionResult Merge([FromBody] Cart a, [FromBody] Cart b) => Ok();
choices: Controllers must return `ActionResult<T>` when they bind a body
Each cart must be a record, since classes cannot bind from JSON
The body is read once, so only one parameter may bind from it
`[FromBody]` is only allowed on actions that accept GET requests
questions.why: The request body is a stream read once by one input formatter, so an action may have at most one `[FromBody]` parameter. Wrap both carts in one DTO, such as `record MergeRequest(Cart A, Cart B)`.
questions.asked: A common beginner error that shows whether you understand how bodies are bound.

questions.q: In Development you want emails written to the console instead of sent. Which registration does that cleanly?
choices: It fails, because services cannot depend on the environment
It works: the environment is known before services are built
It works only if `ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT` is set in appsettings.json
It registers both, so every email is written and sent in Development
questions.why: `builder.Environment` is available while you register services, so picking an implementation per environment is straightforward. The environment comes from `ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT` or `DOTNET_ENVIRONMENT`, not appsettings, and only one branch runs.
questions.asked: Everyday wiring that keeps side effects out of local development.

questions.q: An ASP.NET Core app serves a React SPA from wwwroot. Refreshing on `/orders/42` returns 404. What fixes it?
choices: `app.MapFallbackToFile("index.html")` after the API routes
`app.UseDefaultFiles()`, which maps every unknown path to index.html
A 404 exception handler that redirects to the home page
Adding a controller action for every route the SPA defines
questions.why: Client-side routes do not exist on the server, so unmatched paths must return the SPA's `index.html` and let the router take over. `MapFallbackToFile` does that for anything no other endpoint matched. `UseDefaultFiles` only serves index.html for directory requests.
questions.asked: Hosting a SPA with the API is common; this checks you know how deep links work.

questions.q: A new project calls `builder.Services.AddControllers();`, but requests to controller routes all return 404. What is missing?
choices: `[ApiController]` on every controller, or routes are ignored
`app.UseEndpoints()`, which .NET 8 still requires for routing
`builder.Services.AddRouting()`, which AddControllers does not call
`app.MapControllers()`, which maps their attribute routes
questions.why: `AddControllers` registers the services; `MapControllers` adds the controller endpoints to routing. Without it no controller route exists, hence 404. Routing services are already registered, and `[ApiController]` changes behaviour, not discovery.
questions.asked: A quick check on the services-versus-pipeline split in Program.cs.

questions.q: A handler has a dictionary of field errors. Which result sends a 400 in the standard validation problem format?
choices: `TypedResults.BadRequest(errors)`, which wraps them as ProblemDetails
`TypedResults.ValidationProblem(errors)`
`TypedResults.Problem(errors.ToString())`
`TypedResults.Conflict(errors)`, always used for duplicates
