questions.why: `ValidationProblem` returns `HttpValidationProblemDetails` with status 400 and an `errors` map, the same shape `[ApiController]` produces, so clients handle both alike. `BadRequest(errors)` just serialises the dictionary. Some teams use 409 for duplicates, but not in this format.
questions.asked: Consistent error shapes are a big part of a usable API.

questions.q: How does ASP.NET Core handle an uploaded file bound to `IFormFile` by default?
choices: It streams the file straight to the handler without storing it
It keeps the whole file in memory, however large it is
It buffers it, spilling to a temp file beyond 64 KB
It rejects files over 64 KB unless streaming is enabled
questions.why: Form files are buffered before the handler runs: small ones in memory, larger ones to temporary disk files. That is simple but costly for very large uploads, where streaming with `MultipartReader` (or direct-to-storage uploads) is better.
questions.asked: Upload handling reveals whether you have considered memory and disk under load.

questions.q: What does .NET 9's `app.MapStaticAssets()` add over the older `UseStaticFiles()`?
choices: Build-time compression and fingerprinted URLs with long caching
Server-side rendering of static HTML files before they are sent
Automatic authorisation checks on every static file request
Hosting static files in a CDN without any configuration at all
questions.why: `MapStaticAssets` uses build-time metadata to serve pre-compressed files, strong ETags and fingerprinted URLs that can be cached aggressively and bust on change. `UseStaticFiles` still works but does less at build time. Neither applies authorisation by default.
questions.asked: Shows you keep up with how modern ASP.NET Core serves front-end assets.

questions.q: In .NET 10, what does `builder.Services.AddValidation()` enable for minimal APIs?
questions.code:
record CreateUser([Required] string Name, [EmailAddress] string Email);
app.MapPost("/users", (CreateUser u) => TypedResults.Ok(u));
choices: Validation of the response body before it is sent to the client
DataAnnotations checks on bound parameters, with a 400 on failure
FluentValidation rules discovered automatically from the assembly
Checks on configuration options once the host has started
questions.why: From .NET 10, minimal APIs can validate DataAnnotations on parameters and their types, returning a validation problem response before the handler runs; earlier versions needed a filter or a library. It does not validate responses or run FluentValidation.
questions.asked: Tracks a notable gap closed in .NET 10; candidates on older versions should know the workaround.

questions.q: Which OpenAPI version does `Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi` generate by default in .NET 10?
choices: Swagger 2.0, for compatibility with older tools
OpenAPI 3.0, the same default as in .NET 9
OpenAPI 3.1, aligned with modern JSON Schema
It needs `OpenApiVersion` set, with no default
questions.why: .NET 9 introduced built-in document generation targeting OpenAPI 3.0; .NET 10 moved the default to 3.1, which uses JSON Schema 2020-12 (for example, nullable types via type arrays). You can still choose 3.0 in the options for older tooling.
questions.asked: Relevant when generating clients: schema changes between 3.0 and 3.1 affect tools.

questions.q: What does this .NET 10 minimal API endpoint send?
questions.code:
app.MapGet("/prices", (PriceFeed feed, CancellationToken ct) =>
    TypedResults.ServerSentEvents(feed.StreamAsync(ct)));
choices: A JSON array written once the feed completes
A WebSocket upgrade, then a message per price
A single event, after which the connection closes
A `text/event-stream` response, an event per item
questions.why: `ServerSentEvents` writes each item from the async sequence as an SSE event over a long-lived HTTP response, which browsers read with `EventSource`. It is one-way and simpler than WebSockets or SignalR for live feeds.
questions.asked: A newer built-in option for real-time updates; knowing when it beats SignalR is a plus.

questions.q: A GET handler sets an `ETag` header. With no caching middleware, what happens when a client repeats the request with a matching `If-None-Match`?
choices: ASP.NET Core returns 304 automatically for every endpoint
The handler runs and returns 200 with the full body again
Kestrel returns 412, as the precondition matched the ETag
The browser skips the request and never contacts the server
questions.why: For API endpoints, conditional GET is your code's job: compare `If-None-Match` with the current ETag and return 304 when they match. Static files and some caching features do it for you, but a plain handler does not. 412 is for failed `If-Match` preconditions.
questions.asked: Checks you understand conditional requests beyond knowing the header names.

questions.q: With Asp.Versioning configured as `ReportApiVersions = true`, what do clients see?
choices: Headers listing supported and deprecated versions
A redirect from any old version to the newest version's URL
A 410 Gone for every request to a deprecated version
The version number appended to every JSON response body
questions.why: The library adds `api-supported-versions` and `api-deprecated-versions` headers, so clients can discover upgrades. Deprecated versions keep working until you remove them; nothing is redirected or rewritten.
questions.asked: Communicating deprecation is as important as versioning itself.

questions.q: A video endpoint should support seeking in the browser's player. What should it return?
choices: `TypedResults.Bytes(File.ReadAllBytes(path), "video/mp4")` in memory
A JSON object with the video encoded as a Base64 string
A 302 to a `file://` path the browser can open locally
`PhysicalFile(path, "video/mp4", enableRangeProcessing: true)`
questions.why: Range processing honours `Range` headers with 206 Partial Content, which players use to seek and resume. Loading the whole file into a byte array wastes memory, Base64 inflates it by a third, and `file://` URLs point at the client's own disk.
questions.asked: Serving large files well is a practical skill with memory and UX consequences.

questions.q: An export builds a 500 MB CSV and returns it with `TypedResults.File(bytes, "text/csv")`. What is the main problem?
choices: The whole file sits in memory per request; stream it instead
`File` results are limited to 100 MB and are truncated silently
CSV is not an allowed content type for file results
The response is buffered to disk, so the first byte is slow
questions.why: A byte array holds the entire export in memory, and a few concurrent exports can exhaust the server. Write rows directly to the response body stream, or use a `Stream` overload, so memory stays flat. There is no size cap or content-type restriction.
questions.asked: Exports are a common source of memory spikes; streaming is the expected answer.

questions.q: A service needs the URL of the `GetOrder` endpoint for an email link, without hard-coding the route. What does ASP.NET Core provide?
choices: `IUrlHelper`, injected as a singleton into any service
`HttpContext.Request.Path`, which holds every route template
`LinkGenerator.GetUriByName("GetOrder", new { id }, ...)` from DI
`EndpointDataSource.Find("GetOrder")`, which returns a URL string
questions.why: `LinkGenerator` is a DI service that builds paths or absolute URIs from endpoint names and route values, inside or outside a request. It keeps links correct when routes change. `IUrlHelper` is tied to a request's action context.
questions.asked: Generating links from names avoids brittle string URLs across the codebase.

questions.q: A NuGet library must add a middleware at the very start of every consumer's pipeline without them editing Program.cs. What mechanism exists for this?
choices: An `IStartupFilter` registered in DI, which wraps the pipeline
A static constructor that calls `app.Use` on the running app
An `IHostedService` that inserts middleware once the app starts
A module initialiser that edits the compiled Program class
questions.why: `IStartupFilter.Configure` receives the next configure delegate and can add middleware before (or after) the app's own, which is how some libraries plug in early. Use it sparingly, as hidden middleware surprises readers of Program.cs.
questions.asked: A deeper extensibility point; knowing it exists helps when debugging 'where did this middleware come from?'.

questions.q: You enable HTTP/3 on Kestrel, yet browsers keep using HTTP/2. Which requirement is most often missed?
choices: HTTP/3 only works for requests without cookies or auth
Clients find HTTP/3 via `Alt-Svc`, and need TLS and UDP
HTTP/3 requires the app to be published with Native AOT
HTTP/3 is used only when the port number is 3000 or above
questions.why: HTTP/3 runs over QUIC on UDP and always uses TLS; browsers usually connect with HTTP/2 first and switch after seeing `Alt-Svc`. Firewalls or load balancers that block UDP, or a missing HTTPS endpoint, keep clients on HTTP/2. The OS also needs QUIC support.
questions.asked: Shows you understand protocol negotiation rather than just flipping a setting.

questions.q: A PUT sends `If-Match: "v7"`, but the resource's current ETag is `"v8"`. What should the API return?
choices: 409 Conflict, with the latest version of the resource attached
304 Not Modified, since the client already has a version
200 OK, applying the update because the resource exists
412 Precondition Failed, as the version check failed
questions.why: `If-Match` makes the update conditional; a mismatch means someone changed it first, and RFC 9110 specifies 412. It is the HTTP form of optimistic concurrency, often backed by a row version. 409 is a common choice for conflicts without preconditions; 304 applies to GETs.
questions.asked: Links HTTP semantics to concurrency control, a sign of solid API design.
